items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 《33》以基督受难年龄为轴，构建十二段电声循环，探讨创造、道成肉身、死亡与重生。Yara Mekawei 与 Amir Rezk 取材于圣经段落、科普特正教礼仪与阿拉伯语吟诵，却刻意将文本拆解拉伸，使圣文沦为节奏与质感。低频嗡鸣、失真管弦音色、颗粒化处理与反复断裂重组的打击乐贯穿始终，密度时而压迫、时而骤降至裸露的单薄人声与电子残响。作者将人声与器乐同等视为电子加工素材，使音节化为脉冲、吟诵沦为噪声，模糊了可懂与抽象的边界。专辑结构以《约翰福音》的"太初有道"起始，至《启示录》的新耶路撒冷终结，跨越圣餐、十字架、下冥府与哀悼诸节，形成罕见的连贯灵性轨迹，却绝非逐字重述经典。古老文本在此被当作仍在发声、可被碎裂与栖居的活性素材处理。

items.body: The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision The Getaway by Unterm Rad   Mike Slansky, operating as Unterm Rad, continues his run of punishing industrial IDM with The Getaway for the ever-consistent Bulgaria-based Mahorka imprint. With a background spanning audio engineering, expansive sound design, and graphic work reaching back to the Tympanik Audio era, Slansky was also a key component of the now-shuttered Point Source Electronic Arts collective. His work has long occupied darker electronic spaces, and The Getaway pushes further into that territory through an unusually constrained process: the album was composed entirely from short instrument clips and sounds supplied through Point Source’s Genome sample kits, each fragment carefully edited, processed, and sequenced until it evolved into something entirely new. No synthesizers, AI, or outside sound sources were used, adhering to the open-source spirit of the Genome project. Seven original pieces emerge as dark-grey slabs of machinery, where microscopic edits and fractured rhythms give each track a strangely extraterrestrial charge. Up front, “Hang Me Out To Dry” drives through minimal industrial fissures with a beat-heavy barrage of rugged technoid tones, metallic grit, and tightly controlled distortion. “They’re On To Us” narrows the focus further, exposing Slansky’s precision-built rhythmic glitches as tiny mechanical movements seem to twitch beneath the surface, while “Cornered” opens into broken beats and cavernous echoes, giving the record a sense of mechanical engineer​ing operating somewhere far beyond human reach. Transparent details become increasingly exposed :: The final six pieces hand Slansky’s material over to Access to Arasaka, Evaluation Copy, Vaag, Feederwire, Hexalyne, and Cole, each pulling the source tracks into a distinct interpretation. Rather than simply extending the album, these remixes reveal just how much microscopic movement exists inside Slansky’s sound structures. Access to Arasaka and Hexalyne sharpen the material into brisk, erratic sci-fi electro-nics; Evaluation Copy scorches through beats and bass; Vaag bends the rhythms into flexible broken beat contortions; and Feederwire drags everything through piercing industrial low-end vibrations. Cole’s closing interpretation is perhaps the most surreal, stripping the machinery back until its strange, transparent details become increasingly exposed. The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Closing with “The Walls Are Closing In,” before the remixes kick in, Slansky lets pressure evaporate into sparse technoid shifts, leaving behind an album that feels both rigorously engineered and strangely alive. By opening his source material to collaborators, he turns a tightly controlled sonic experiment into a broader study of industrial texture, glitch mechanics, and extraterrestrial electronics—chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision. The Getaway is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] The Getaway by Unterm RadThe post Unterm Rad :: The Getaway (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Unterm Rad 的《The Getaway》是一张全程在严格限制条件下完成的工业 IDM 作品：所有声音均来自 Point Source 的 Genome 样本包片段，经过显微级别的切片、变形与重组，最终凝成七首充满机械感与异域信号的暗灰色音块。评论特别强调制作过程中对短样本的精细编辑与节奏干扰，使每首曲目都呈现出类似外星传输的变异质感。专辑后半部分邀请六位电子音乐人以混音形式拆解原作，暴露出原始素材内部隐藏的微观律动——Access to Arasaka 与 Hexalyne 走向锋利科幻电子，Evaluation Copy 加重低频冲击，Vaag 拉伸出破碎节拍的弹性扭曲，Feederwire 注入工业低频共振，结尾 Cole 的版本则将机械骨架剥离至近乎透明的残片。整体上，这张作品在小厂牌 Mahorka 框架下完成了对工业声响边界的一次精密探索。

items.body: Strikkland are easy to misread if you mistake humour for distance. Henrik Johansson can deliver brutal lyrics while smiling, appear in a red feather boa, play with national flags or deliberately puncture the visual severity traditionally associated with EBM, but none of that suggests embarrassment about the genre. Quite the opposite. The joke works because the attachment underneath it is genuine. They are not standing outside EBM making fun of its conventions; they know those conventions intimately enough to interfere with them. I first saw the Gothenburg duo at E-Only in 2024 and again this year on the much larger Waldbühne at Nocturnal Culture Night. At NCN, something became particularly clear: humour had stopped feeling like something happening around the songs and had become part of Strikkland’s performance language itself. Hard electronic structures, Henrik’s forceful delivery and the physical directness of EBM remained intact, while gestures, costumes and irony continually destabilised the expectation that seriousness must look solemn. Their second album, “Hommage”, makes that tension especially interesting. It openly acknowledges the music that formed Henrik and Henric, while its production deliberately returns to hardware, physical studio equipment and recording practices associated with an earlier era. Yet Strikkland have little interest in turning EBM into heritage preservation. For them, tradition is useful precisely when it can still be disturbed. We spoke about growing into a band after fifty, refusing genre uniforms, why limitation can generate creativity, the ethics of AI, the strange authority of old symbols, and what happens when two people who take EBM very seriously refuse to behave as though seriousness requires a permanent scowl. Strikkland interview Karo: I first saw you at E-Only in 2024 and then again on the much larger Waldbühne at NCN this year. What struck me at NCN was how much more clearly humour had become part of the performance language itself. When did you realise that humour could be structural to Strikkland rather than merely something happening between songs? Henrik: We have always had humour as an important element of what Strikkland is all about. We started the band on impulse and as a fun thing to do. The lyrics are often conjured up at the same time as we are in the studio creating new songs. My texts often tend to drift towards dark stories about space, death, fantasy and the absurd. The humour you get from seeing the band live is something we have developed throughout all the time we have been on stage. We have fun, and that creates what we deliver. Henric: We realised early on that two old geezers would only look ridiculous if we tried to act tougher or darker than we actually are. Besides, there are plenty of bands already biting heads off chickens or dressing up in full combat gear on stage. It has all been done before, and it really didn’t seem like an option for us. Our appearance and the way we behave also evolved from criticism in Sweden after our first live shows in the early days: “Their music is half-decent, but they aren’t a real EBM band because they don’t look or behave like one.” We kind of turned that against the critics, embraced it even more and made it our thing. Karo: At NCN you told me that when you started the band, already approaching your fifties, you briefly considered becoming the “gothiest” band possible before deciding that pretending to be something you were not would be ridiculous. Did starting Strikkland later in life actually give you a kind of freedom younger bands sometimes lack, because you had less need to prove that you belonged? Henrik: Absolutely! Also, later in life you have so many more musical influences to choose from and try to implement into your own songs. Starting a band later in life also means you can afford to have a band and go places to play live without starving and sleeping in the car on the way there. We are doing something today that you thought impossible when you were young. Henric: Being close to 50 when you start a band certainly provides more freedom. Our ambition was never to release records or perform live, but when possibilities opened up, we jumped for it. Speaking for myself, I got a chance to do what I wanted to do in my teens but never got the chance to do. At 50, you aren’t as afraid of criticism or about what others might think as you are at 16 or 17. That helped a lot. Karo: EBM has accumulated a very strict visual and behavioural vocabulary: severity, discipline, confrontation, often a certain cultivated lack of humour. You clearly love the genre, but you also interfere with those conventions constantly. Which parts of EBM do you take completely seriously, and which parts do you think deserve to be laughed at? Henrik: We never laugh at EBM, but we think we can involve irony and humour in the genre and have a laugh at certain aspects of life. Humour and art are always found in the contrasts. I mostly write quite dark lyrics, but we present them with a lot of smiles, humour and dance. Henric: EBM has been a huge part of my life since the 1980s, so it is something I take very seriously. I do laugh at some of the rigidity coming from certain corners of the fanbase, though. Come on, loosen up and dance while you still can. Have fun. At least laugh a little. There are enough bitter middle-aged men in the world, and I don’t want to become one of them. Karo: That is also why “Hommage” interests me. It is explicitly a tribute to the music that formed you, but homage can easily become imitation. How do you honour an artistic language without treating it as something that should remain frozen in the period when you first discovered it? Henrik: The tribute to the EBM bands we grew up with is always there when we make music. In “Hommage”, it is in the basslines, the sounds, the technology and the artwork. I am a curious person, so I constantly look for new music and new bands to listen to. The EBM genre, and Strikkland, keep finding new ways without letting go of the legacy of the bands of the 80s. Henric: Apart from a handful of gems from bands like Kraftwerk, DAF, Nitzer Ebb, Front 242 and a few others which can’t be topped, EBM and electronic music have evolved a lot. In my playlists there are rarely any songs older than two or three years. You can still hear where it is coming from, but it has evolved. If we stick to what we grew up with, there would be stagnation and the genre would surely die out. But thanks to artists like SIIE, Emmon, Plastikstrom and many others, it is still interesting. So I would rather risk going outside the standard formula and at least try to contribute to keeping EBM alive, both musically and visually. Karo: You made “Hommage” deliberately with classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines, and you were very explicit about not using AI. Is that primarily an ethical position, an aesthetic one, or did you simply want the limitations of those tools to become part of the composition? Henric: AI has no place in art. Full stop. For both creative and ethical reasons. When it comes to using hardware versus working “in the box”, it is purely a workflow decision. The tactility of turning knobs and pushing buttons works better for me than using plugins. We are also privileged enough to get to work together with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, which is both a studio and a “synthesizer museum”. It would be stupid not to use all of those classic machines if you can. Our first album, “Bodypop”, was mixed there on an SSL 4000E console, so when we got the chance to mix “Hommage” at Hansa in Berlin on their SSL console, of course we took the plunge. And of course we did some additional recordings there as well. I mean, who could resist playing the very same Steinway grand piano that Martin Gore posed in his jocks next to? Karo: There is an interesting contradiction there: Strikkland describe themselves as expanding the borders of EBM, yet “Hommage” deliberately looks backwards in terms of production practice. Can technological limitation actually be more progressive than unlimited technological possibility? Henrik: Well, maybe in a way every EBM band today is expanding the borders of EBM? To stay in the genre, you have to remain within the frame agreed upon, regardless of what technology you use. But it gets more interesting if you drift away towards the border and sometimes cross it, bringing in other influences and expressions. That’s the way music has always evolved. Henric: For me, limitation sparks creativity. There is a certain number of available channels on a physical mixing console. On a computer, you can have hundreds. There are also limitations to hardware synthesizers and effects, and all of this forces me to be creative. As mentioned before, this is a workflow that suits me. With that said, most of our songs start out “in the box” because it is convenient. Karo: Henric writes the music and programming while Henrik handles vocals and lyrics. With such a clear division, where does the personality of a Strikkland song emerge? Does the music arrive with a character already inside it, or can the vocal idea fundamentally alter what Henric thought he had written? Henrik: Often we start with a bassline that Henric has created and then build it together from that point. I get inspiration for the lyrics and write them at the same time as Henric starts to develop the music. When both of us feel ready, we fuse it all together. This is a fast process, so we are very much in line with what kind of music we want to produce. Henric: Let’s put it this way: when Henrik enters the studio, I might have 20 loops that I have worked on for six months, with basslines, drums and maybe a melody ready. If Henrik says, “Great! But can we change this or that?”, that loop goes into the bin. But if he stops, shuts up and starts to write text immediately, I know it is a keeper. Then we combine that idea into a draft by making a rough arrangement, tweaking the text, tweaking the music and finally recording it. When we have enough tracks for an album, we take it to Hans and re-record everything. So, to answer your question, the music inspires the vocals and the vocals give direction to the final piece of music. Neither would be the same without the other. Karo: At NCN, Henrik changed clothes, exaggerated gestures and played with Swedish and German symbols and declarations of friendship. In a genre that has historically borrowed heavily from militarised imagery, does humour give you a way to use those symbols without allowing them to retain all of their old authority? Henrik: When I go to see a band live, I want to be entertained. When I am on stage, I want to entertain and have a good time! To joke around and interact with the audience and get a warm response elates me. I love the contrast of delivering hard-hitting music and brutal lyrics with a smile on my face and prancing around with a red feather boa. So yes, it is absolutely a way to deflate the power of symbols of power. Henric: Personally, I think it is important to reclaim symbols like national flags from fascists and extremists and use them in a positive way. We don’t hide behind humour and irony, but instead use them as tools for communication. Our message is clear. We don’t accept fascists, Nazis or totalitarian regimes, we support Ukraine’s fight for freedom and we advocate free speech. But maybe we have chosen a “lighter approach” to convey this than other bands, mainly because the darker image doesn’t suit us on a personal level. Karo: What I particularly liked was that none of this reduced the concert to parody because the musical foundation remained genuinely hard. Do you consciously protect that balance, making sure the joke never becomes an excuse for musical weakness? Henrik: When we make our music, we never implement humour to start with. Okay, some lyrics are rather absurd and some sound effects we add for fun, but we want our music to be serious and taken seriously. It is mostly when we play live that we joke around. Henric: Some people have clearly written us off as a parody act. No question about that! But either they haven’t seen us perform live or they haven’t understood what we are doing. Irony is a tough nut to crack for some, and others lack humour. One thing is certain, though. We would never release or perform anything that we ourselves thought was weak, and we put a lot of work into our music. Karo: You worked with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion and Hansa Studios on “Hommage”. Did working in spaces carrying so much recording history make you more conscious of tradition, or was the important thing precisely to forget the mythology once you were actually inside the studio? Henric: It took a while for it to sink in once we were at Hansa. We were actually sitting at the same mixing console that was used to make some of the greatest albums of my youth?! Insane! But once that feeling disappeared, it was just another day in the studio and we did our thing together with Hans. Henrik: Hans Olsson suggested mixing the album at Hansa, and I honestly was totally unaware of the history of this studio. Henric was jumping up and down with excitement. We were there for three days and it finally dawned on me how cool it was! There we could use the same machines and instruments that our heroes used. Karo: The larger stage at NCN seemed to suit you surprisingly well. Some electronic acts compensate for space by simply making every gesture bigger; with Strikkland, the additional room seemed to expose more of the interaction between you. Has playing larger stages changed the way you understand what the visual side of the band can do? Henric: We are not that used to playing larger stages. Apart from Subkultfestivalen in Sweden and WGT, most of our shows prior to NCN have been in front of a maximum of 200 to 300 people. I think there is a lot of room for visual improvement when playing the larger stages. We are just two guys and a couple of machines, so in order to put on even better shows we probably need some additional features on stage to make an impact. But we also don’t want to hide behind video walls, smoke and lasers. Guess it’s time to put on our thinking caps and find a Strikkland solution to the problem. But yeah, visuals are important to us, from album covers to how we appear on stage. Henrik: What Henric said. Karo: “Hommage” looked deliberately towards the music that made you. Looking ahead, what would be the opposite gesture? Is there something in the EBM tradition, perhaps even something you personally love, that Strikkland now need to leave behind in order to find out what the band can become next? Henrik: I can’t think of a thing in the EBM tradition that we want to leave behind. When we create new songs, all kinds of new influences colour the final result. Last time we met, the song rotated towards techno music, so who knows? I always get new ideas every time I listen to metal music. There you find my inspiration and trigger to do new stuff for Strikkland. But with that said, there will never be a guitar on stage with us. Body music forever! Henric: I don’t know, to be honest. There are most certainly no holy cows as far as Strikkland is concerned. What we would love to happen is to do even more shows in mainland Europe, and if that means we will have to tweak things one way or another, so be it. If it turns out we have to bite heads off chickens or perform in Pickelhauben in order to get booked, it might be worth a shot! I mean, a lot of people do judge books by the cover, and it would be sad to miss out because of that. We will see what happens and what we come up with. About Strikkland Strikkland are an electronic body music duo from Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of Henric Ceder, responsible for music and programming, and Henrik Johansson, responsible for vocals and lyrics. Their first documented release, “Predatorial Right”, appeared on 27 March 2020. Their debut full-length album, “Bodypop”, followed on 2 December 2022. The ten-track record was mixed and mastered by Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, using an analogue SSL 4000E console; Strikkland explicitly connected that production choice to their admiration for classic EBM. Their second full-length, “Hommage”, was released on 28 March 2025. The nine-track album was produced by Hans Olsson, with recording, mixing and mastering work carried out at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg and Hansa Studios in Berlin. The band describe the album as a tribute both to the artists who inspired them and to older recording practices. They state that no AI was used in its production, relying instead primarily on classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines.
items._cn_summary: Strikkland是来自瑞典哥德堡的二人EBM组合，他们的第二张专辑《Hommage》展现了独特的音乐理念：以幽默解构传统EBM的严肃性。Henrik与Henric两位成员年过五十后组建乐队，以戏谑态度挑战电子工业音乐的类型惯例。制作上刻意回归硬件设备和早期录音方式，向影响他们的前辈致敬，但并非怀旧复刻，而是让传统在当代语境中继续被激活。舞台上，他们用红色羽毛围巾、国旗道具等视觉元素打破观众对EBM的刻板期待，同时保留了硬朗的电子结构、有力的演唱和直接的物理感。这张专辑的核心张力在于：真正尊重类型的人，恰恰能够以幽默方式对其进行干扰；传统只有在仍可被打破时才具有生命力。

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. Pick up a copy in our online shop. Subscribers can read the full article in the digital archive here.

items._cn_summary: 这是斯洛文尼亚钢琴家Kaja Draksler为The Wire杂志制作的独家混音作品。作为阿姆斯特丹音乐学院出身的即兴音乐人，她的创作路径偏离传统爵士正统，融合了学院派即兴与当代音乐的多重脉络。混音以拼贴手法呈现，将不同作品的片段依次拼接甚至叠加，曲目涵盖她自己的创作与所欣赏的音乐，焦点集中于钢琴与人声。选曲跨越爵士、古典、当代作曲与流行边界，包括Luciano Berio的声乐作品、Pauline Oliveros的实验人声、Cecil Taylor与Craig Taborn的钢琴即兴、Nina Simone的经典，以及阿塞拜疆mugham传统的Vaqif Mustafazadeh。整体展现出对声音材料的高度敏感与跨类型审美的开阔视野，是一份带有策展意识的声音文献。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.
items._cn_summary: Michael Mantler 1976年专辑将Edward Gorey的暗黑童话故事与爵士融合音乐相结合，邀请Robert Wyatt担任叙述者，联合Jack DeJohnette、Terje Rypdal、Carla Bley与Steve Swallow等爵士即兴高手共同演绎。专辑采用文学叙事加配乐的模式，叙述者的朗诵与乐队的反应式演奏形成松散而动态的互动，乐手们以吉他、风琴、合成弦乐和打击乐构建出戏剧性的声场氛围。编曲手法兼顾即兴自由与结构编排，后半部分曲目开始展现更完整的作曲思维，包括复杂节奏织体与戏剧性配器段落。该作品在爵士与前卫摇滚之间找到平衡点，将叙事性音乐推向实验性领域。

items.body: With Hor-Cheret, we welcome a new project presented as a collaboration between members of Vortex, Nam-Khar, and Delta Komplex, complemented by a few more artists. The project’s name alludes to Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. With an album title referring to an ancient nomadic law of hospitality, Hor-Cheret offers an intriguing metaphor and, in my view, a critical perspective on today’s world. It certainly offers food for thought, but above all, this is music to be discovered. From the very first notes, a distinct Ritual influence emerges through the percussion and the use of traditional acoustic instruments. While the percussion reinforces the album’s ritualistic character, the listener gradually discovers a dark atmosphere shaped by deep sound waves. Elements of Dark-Ambient and Industrial music are clearly present. An Ethereal female voice occasionally takes on a narrative role while simultaneously enhancing the sense of mysticism. The male voice also serves a narrative function, while some of the lyrics possess a distinctly poetic quality. This is a superbly crafted album in a genre that suffers from a lack of quality projects and inconsistent production standards. Hor-Cheret’s debut is a release to be savored and cherished. (Rating:8½). Listen to “In The Shadow Ov Power”: In The Shadow Ov Power by HOR-CHERET About Hor-Cheret Hor-Cheret is a new collaborative project pairing members of Vortex, Nam-Khar and Delta Komplex with additional contributors, presented on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Its name references Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. Nam-Khar is the ritual ambient project of Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009, previously paired with Vortex on “Nag-Hammadi” in 2022 and “The Sarajevo Spiral” in 2024. Delta Komplex is a German electronic band founded in 2019 around Minu-Schirin Samimi and Tufana, known for the 2022 album “Veils”. “Nanawatai”, Hor-Cheret’s debut album, was released on 7 November 2025 in a limited handnumbered digipak edition.
items._genre: ritual ambient / dark ambient / industrial / neofolk
items._cn_summary: Hor-Cheret是由Vortex、Nam-Khar和Delta Komplex成员联合发起的合作项目，首张专辑《Nanawatai》以埃及神话中Horus之名呼应古代游牧部落的待客法则，对当下世界做出隐喻性批判。音乐层面以打击乐与传统原声乐器构建强烈的仪式感基底，深沉的声波塑造出黑暗氛围，融合Dark-Ambient与工业元素。女声飘逸空灵，承担叙事与神秘感营造；男声同样具有叙事功能，部分歌词充满诗意。整体制作精良，在仪式氛围音乐这一品质参差不齐的领域中展现出罕见的完成度与深度，是一张值得反复品味的作品。

items.body: Two pizzas, a boombox, and a demo CD-R were enough to keep Michael Mayer and Wolfgang Voigt out all night. In Mayer’s recollection, their first encounter with the music of young Regensburg producer Markus Guentner began in a Cologne park. The listening session continued as they wandered through the city, playing the same three tracks over and over. Something in those recordings had altered the evening sufficiently that neither man wanted to switch them off. “We knew that we had found something outrageously beautiful and we wanted the whole world to listen,” Mayer recalls. A quarter-century later, that encounter offers a useful way into In Moll. Music associated with introspection and solitude first won over two of its most consequential listeners in the open air, among streets and other people. It could change the character of a place, and the quality of the time spent there. As the album’s 25th anniversary is celebrated this September, those possibilities remain central to its appeal. Its return through Rafael Anton Irisarri’s Black Knoll Editions on November 6, 2026 also brings a substantial restoration: the complete album will finally be available on vinyl, including the previously omitted “In Moll 4.” The photographs from around the album’s creation bring its history back to an everyday scale. There are headphones around Guentner’s neck, rows of mixer controls, a Technics T-shirt, and him as a young man sitting on a sofa with his arms folded. They place a face and familiar surroundings beside music often discussed in terms of vastness. Guentner was about twenty when In Moll appeared. Its compositional assurance can make that easy to forget. Markus Guentner around the time of In Moll’s original release. His Regensburg EP had appeared on Kompakt in 2000. “Regensburg 1” and “Pilot” followed on the inaugural Pop Ambient 2001 compilation, alongside music by Dettinger, Ulf Lohmann, Joachim Spieth, and others. The series gave a name and a shared home to an area of experimentation within the label’s wider electronic community. Melody could remain immediate even as the familiar structures of a song dissolved; repetition could carry an emotional charge without being organized around a dancefloor payoff. Kompakt’s account of Pop Ambient emphasizes pop as an attitude, connected to subculture and Pop Art. That distinction helps recover the uncertainty and excitement of the early records. Producers were investigating what happened when the machinery of club music was allowed to move at another pace. A phrase might expand until its texture became as absorbing as its tune. Bass could give weight to an otherwise suspended passage. The space surrounding a sound became part of the composition. In Moll belongs to the cultural interval those experiments opened up. In the chillout and comedown era, electronic music had acquired a life in the hours surrounding the club: the quiet room, the trip home, the morning when exhilaration gave way to more complicated feelings. Dub minimalism’s treatment of bass and empty space met a distinctly post-industrial sadness. Guentner gave that meeting an unusually intimate form, allowing warmth and unease to occupy the same stretch of music. Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS was an obvious contemporary reference point, with its dense textures and softened rhythmic presence. Guentner developed a more private expression within related territory. In his April 2002 review for Pitchfork, Mark Richardson recognized the connection while drawing attention to the album’s industrial unease and enclosed spaces. That early response is useful now: the music’s beauty has always accommodated discomfort. Its emotional proximity to post-punk is easy to understand. Solitude, urban stillness, and longing held under restraint have sustained entire bodies of work in that tradition. In Moll, whose title translates as “in minor,” gives those feelings an electronic form. The low frequencies suggest weight and distance; small melodic details offer something close enough to hold. Melancholy becomes a relationship between the individual and the space around them. You can imagine the deserted street as readily as the room overlooking it. That relationship gives the ten-minute “In Moll 3” particular significance. The album’s most popular track, selected as the anniversary edition’s second single, is an especially apt introduction to its darker emotional register. Its heavy synthesizer layers and deep echo give it a substantial, almost architectural presence. Within that scale, the melodic pull remains personal. The tension between those qualities helps explain how a piece of such duration can become the record listeners return to most readily. Ten minutes also allows a different kind of encounter with a piece of music. A feeling can occupy the foreground, recede, and become apparent again as attention shifts. For listeners drawn to coldwave’s inward concentration or dream pop’s prolonged emotional suspension, “In Moll 3” offers a natural point of entry. Its place at the centre of this anniversary campaign makes sense: it gives newcomers enough time to discover the album’s proportions, and returning listeners a reason to settle into them again. Watch the visualizer for “In Moll 3,” with music and video by Markus Guentner, below: Born in Regensburg, Germany, in 1981, Markus Guentner discovered electronic music at thirteen and secured his first weekly DJ residency while still a teenager. His listening extended across shoegaze, dream pop, indie rock, pop, ambient, and techno, giving him an appreciation for both the directness of a melody and the expressive possibilities of texture. Those interests informed a musical life rooted in his hometown, where he later co-founded the SUBLIME collective in 2006. The connection to the broader post-punk family also has a concrete history. In 2005, Guentner worked with 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell on The Hope Blister’s Underarms and Sideways, supplying the reworkings that formed its second disc. His version of Talk Talk’s “Such a Shame,” featuring Dana Grey, had meanwhile carried his affection for pop into a club setting through Ware Records. These projects reflect a musician whose interests could move naturally between a song’s emotional clarity and the possibilities of abstraction. Across releases for Kompakt, Ware, Warner, Sending Orbs, and Affin, Guentner has continued to move between minimal techno, beatless composition, and extended drone. Collaborations with Rafael Anton Irisarri, Julia Kent, Brock Van Wey (bvdub), Joachim Spieth, and zakè have brought other approaches into contact with his own, sustaining an exchange between musicians whose work shares an interest in depth and duration. His association with A Strangely Isolated Place began in 2012 with Talking Clouds, released through the label’s Places Series. Theia followed in 2015, beginning the loosely connected trio of albums completed by Empire and Extropy. These records gave his bass drones and slow melodic developments a larger, cosmic setting. In 2024, Kontrapunkt brought eight collaborations together, with contributors including Arovane, Abul Mogard, Benoît Pioulard, Karen Vogt, and Hollie Kenniff. Guentner’s work also extends into graphic design and cinema. His longstanding partnership with Joachim Spieth includes shaping Affin’s visual identity, while his music has featured in Drake Doremus’ Equals. That attention to the relationship between sound and image continues in the new visual presentation he has designed for In Moll. For Irisarri, the influence of In Moll reaches directly into his own beginnings. He first heard the album shortly after its 2001 release, while still discovering what he wanted to express through electronic music. “Markus showed me entirely new possibilities for what electronic music could communicate,” he recalls. His assessment of its importance to his project The Sight Below is unequivocal: “The Sight Below would not have existed without IN MOLL paving the way.” Brock Van Wey, better known as bvdub, remembers a similarly personal recognition. In his anniversary recollection, he describes hearing an unfamiliar producer articulate feelings he was struggling with far away: “it was as if that album was made to comfort me.” Their eventual friendship brought the additional pleasure of finding kindness in a musician he had admired for years. Such accounts give the word “influence” some substance. A record helped someone feel understood; that listener went on to make music of his own. Irisarri’s stewardship of the anniversary edition gives that history a particularly satisfying continuation. An artist whose possibilities were expanded by In Moll has now undertaken its new analogue remaster. The restoration of “In Moll 4” corrects a long-standing difference between the original formats: the piece was included on CD, while the vinyl edition left it out. Its first appearance on vinyl restores the seven-part sequence to the format, preserving the full span of the work. For an album so dependent on the relationship between duration, density, and release, completeness has an artistic value as well as an archival one. Guentner has also designed a new visual presentation for the edition, extending his involvement beyond the recordings themselves. The album returns with the care of its maker and of a musician it helped inspire. Richardson, looking back in the accompanying press materials, calls it “one of the finest ambient releases of the 00’s.” The strongest argument for that assessment lies in how readily the record can still enter the present. Heard in 2026, its patient pacing and emotional economy feel entirely current. Contemporary interest in slow music and environmental listening gives fresh context to choices Guentner was making twenty-five years ago. He understood how a recording could become part of a room while retaining its own complicated emotional life. In that sense, the world has gradually caught up with In Moll: more listeners have found reasons to seek the concentration and depth it has offered all along. That brings us back to Mayer and Voigt carrying a young producer’s music through Cologne. The circumstances belong to another time; the discovery remains available. Put on In Moll, give it an hour, and notice what happens to the room. In Moll (25th Anniversary Edition) is due November 6, 2026, through Black Knoll Editions (BKE025), with digital and black or white double-vinyl editions available to pre-order. Bandcamp currently lists December shipping estimates for the vinyl. “In Moll 4,” the first single, is available now. Listen below and pre-order the anniversary edition here. items._cn_summary: Markus Guentner 的首张专辑《In Moll》迎来发行二十五周年，首次以完整黑胶形式再版发行，收录此前缺失的第四首曲目。Guentner 创作此专辑时年仅二十岁，作品呈现出远超年龄的成熟与结构掌控力。音乐延续了他在 Kompakt 厂牌发表《Regensburg》EP 时期奠定的方向，旋律保持直入人心的同时剥离了传统歌曲结构，让重复本身承载情感重量。评论将专辑置于 Pop Ambient 系列的文化语境中考量，强调俱乐部之外的电子音乐生活——从安静角落到归途清晨再到情绪复杂的次日。Kompakt 将 Pop 理解为一种态度，关联亚文化与波普艺术，赋予音乐持续实验的空间。声响的空间感被纳入作曲本身，低频为悬置段落赋予重量，纹理与旋律并重。

items.body: Label: Edition Records, 2026 Personnel - Mark Guiliana: drums, percussion, electronics, keyboards, guitar, vocals; Nicholas Semrad: keyboards; Stu Brooks: electric bass (#3), electronics (#2,4,7,8); Tim Lefebvre: electric bass (#2,4,6); Gretchen Parlato: vocals (#4,5); Marley Guiliana: vocals (#5). Mixed feelings arose from listening to Beat Music 2.0 , the synth-infused follow-up to Mark Guiliana’s Grammy-nominated album Beat Music! Beat Music! Beat Music! (Motéma, 2019). Retro and futuristic waves emerge from Guiliana’s compositions, which draw inspiration from early gaming culture and electronic music. Still, the focus here is on human connection and collaboration, as he enlists keyboardist Nicholas Semrad, bassist Tim Lefebvre, vocalist Gretchen Parlato, and Stu Brooks on electronics. The opener, “ B.ANG ”, excavates retro electronic music through glitchy synth ostinatos that march alongside the harmonic progression, along with a mix of ambient undercurrents and Gary Numan-style electro-rock energy. Although it tests the elasticity of the song’s edges, this piece failed to leave a strong impression on me. “ B.ORN ” and “ W.EST ” are also nothing special, while “ D.RUM ”, with its industrial stomp generating controlled trepidation and Parlato’s vocals highlighting the contrasting ambient-leaning passages, has a little more flair. I did feel a spark on numbers like “ P.LAY ”, whose actively propulsive drumming, together with Lefebvre’s brawny bass fluxes and pedals, is nothing short of gravity-defying, and “ B.EAT ”, whose grooving dub atmosphere morphs into club-dance territory for a while. Brooks, who infuses relevant, to-the-point electronics into the former, switches to electric bass on the latter. Also worth mentioning is “ M.OVE ”, whose danceable techno patterns reminded me of 808 State. Cross-rhythmic tides and dramatic shifts make this one a standout. Guiliana’s passion for what he does is undeniable, yet the prevailing virtues of Beat Music 2.0 come to the fore when the layers adopt a less explicit old-school electronic vibe in favor of more modernistic experimentation. Favorite Tracks: 02 - P.LAY ► 03 - B.EAT ► 07 - M.OVE

items._cn_summary: 鼓手Mark Guiliana在《Beat Music 2.0》中将爵士节奏逻辑与电子音乐合成语言深度交织，以早期游戏文化与电子乐传统为灵感，跨越复古与未来两端。专辑以glitch合成器ostinato和工业节奏骨架为基底，融合ambient氛围层与club舞曲律动，在电子纹理中始终保留人声与即兴互动。亮点曲目如《P.LAY》以重低音贝斯与活跃推进的鼓击构筑失重感，《B.EAT》在dub与舞曲之间游走，《M.OVE》则以techno律动与cross-rhythm制造戏剧性张力。相比前作，本作在减少明显复古电子印记的同时，倾向于更现代化的声音实验与层次堆叠，体现出Guiliana对跨领域协作与音色探索的热情。Edition Records发行，独立厂牌加持，适合关注实验电子与爵士交汇的听众。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，与83岁的肯尼亚传统dodo流派歌手Ogoya Nengo合作完成。Nengo的加入为音乐注入了深厚的传统根基，她与Ratengo同住附近、声线交织呼应。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐和架子鼓构建音色层次，合成复节奏以微妙方式层层叠加，既不掩盖人声，也不脱离非洲根源。在《Bara》中，廉价的节拍敲击与歌声形成生硬对照，随后4/4节拍、贝斯线条、木琴音色逐次浮现，至曲末融为一体。《Sarah》则以Ratengo主唱、Kacirek试探性打击点缀，失真音效在声线高潮处切入。乐评指出，此类作品体现了21世纪文化间真诚对话——根源成为前卫，创新仿若古老。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 与意大利作曲家 Francesco Paolo Paladino 及诗人 Luca Chino Ferrari 合作，带来专辑《Songs of Compassion》。十一首作品以钢琴为主轴，配合弦乐、木管、合成器泛音与金属质感音色，营造非线性、非调性中心的声响空间。评论将其比作 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass 的简约重复传统，而非流行摇滚的旋律套路。Moskowitz 的演唱如意识流般起伏，不遵循功能和声进行，而是让每个词的重量自行显现。歌词层面，作品承袭1960年代抗议歌曲传统，《Pale Wanderer》揭示威权主义如何依赖自愿共谋者，《Charlottesville》直接引用游行口号以对抗新纳粹话语；同时亦有关于死亡与人在宇宙中位置的冥想。整体呈现为世界疲惫却清醒的声音，融合政治批判与哲学沉思，在当下政治分裂的语境中回应当年催生其前身的时代精神。

Seun turns the preachers’ own words back on them: on the title track and first single of his upcoming album Na Dem, he already listed reverends, bishops, pastors and imams among the “winch men” he wants saving from, and his father Fela Kuti went after the same pul
items.body: “The devil is busy” is what churchgoers say when trouble arrives, and Seun Kuti & Egypt 80 take the phrase, as “Devil Just Busy”, and point it at the darkness closing over contemporary society. Seun turns the preachers’ own words back on them: on the title track and first single of his upcoming album Na Dem, he already listed reverends, bishops, pastors and imams among the “winch men” he wants saving from, and his father Fela Kuti went after the same pulpits on “Shuffering and Shmiling” in 1978. “DJB” gives the phrase seven minutes of dark, mid-tempo afrobeat, laid down by two drummers, Mario Orsinet and Femi Koleoso, and two bassists, Kunle Justice and Gbeke Ojutiku. Seun sings and plays saxophone on top, with two trumpets and four more saxophones building the horn arrangements around him. Koleoso, who leads Ezra Collective, also produced the track, as he did the whole of Na Dem. Na Dem arrives on 6 November via Django Music, eight days before Fela becomes the first African solo artist inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Seun, who inherited Egypt 80 at 14 when his father died in 1997, will be in Los Angeles to represent him at the ceremony, five weeks after the band play the city’s Regent Theater on 9 October. That date sits in a US run that also takes in Belly Up Tavern in Solana Beach on 7 October, FORM Arcosanti in Arizona and Webster Hall in New York on 14 October. Listen to “DJB” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Seun Kuti & Egypt80 – DJB appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._genre: afrobeat / afrofunk / world music / political commentary
items._cn_summary: Seun Kuti 作为 Fela Kuti 之子，延续了父亲开创的非洲节拍传统。新专辑收录曲《Devil Just Busy》以七分钟中速暗色调编排展开，由两位鼓手与两位贝斯手奠定节奏根基，萨克斯、小号与多支萨克斯组成的铜管阵构建层次。歌词将教会用语翻转，矛头指向当今社会的黑暗面，与父亲 1978 年《Shuffering and Shmiling》批判宗教机构的传统一脉相承。制作人 Femi Koleoso 同时领导 Ezra Collective 爵士乐队，为这首 afrobeat 注入了当代爵士乐的编排思路。专辑由 Django Music 厂牌发行，在 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame 典礼前夕推出，具有特殊的历史纪念意义。整体延续非洲政治音乐脉络，融合传统 afrobeat 与现代爵士制作手法，是世界音乐领域中兼具传承与当代性的作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — At the time, I thought Strange Little Girls was the last album where Tori Amos pursued a specific stylistic direction; just as she had previously dedicated albums to the sound of the acoustic piano or the clavichord, here she focused on the Wurlitzer (alongside her classic B�sendorfer piano), which gave the record a very special atmosphere. Yet that wasn't the only thing distinguishing the �lbum, which was dedicated to covering songs originally performed by men and giving them a feminine twist. However, rather than focusing on the personas she created for each track, I want to concentrate on the music itself; each version is distinct and received such a unique treatment, akin to applying makeup, that the song was transformed until it became unrecognizable, turning into something entirely new. This reveals the true meaning of reimagining a song."New Age", originally by The Velvet Underground, is transported to another dimension: a cold, futuristic realm, ripped without anesthesia from its quasi-hippie, Buffalo Springfield-esque setting. Tori sings with restraint at first before letting go; her voice sounds perfect alongside the album's other star, guitarist Adrian Belew. While the original held the light of morning, she imbued this version with the shadow of dusk, its diametric opposite.Belew helps make the album more challenging and progressive; his riffs complement the spirit of Tori, which was already unconventional for the time. Then there is "'97 Bonnie & Clyde", originally by rapper Eminem, though it goes without saying that the song is unrecognizable here. It is subtle and modern, yet simultaneously evokes the 1920s, featuring a drum machine that contrasts with the sound of violins and her whispered vocals.The case of "Strange Little Girls" is intriguing; for its creators, The Stranglers, it represented a move toward modernity, embracing new wave after their punk past, while Amos takes it a step further by making it postmodern. The Wurlitzer lends a futuristic air, and her committed, uninhibited vocal performance, bolstered by backing vocals, truly makes the song her own. Matt Chamberlain provides the final touch that perfects the power of this rendition.Depeche Mode's "Enjoy the Silence" is so powerful that one need not dig deep to unlock its full potential. Stripped of all its trappings, just the song itself, a piano, and a few strings, it shone like a mineral catching a ray of sunlight, glowing even from afar.She took 10cc's 1975 track "I'm Not In Love", originally warm and even contradictorily (or paradoxically) romantic, and made it icy, almost Krautrock-esque and mechanical; it features a long introduction where the beautiful original melody is recognizable only in her vocals, yet here it feels more like a threat, even though the original lyrics seemed like a confession born of denial."Rattlesnakes", a song by Lloyd Cole and the Commotions, also retains its original melody, though the tempo has been slowed down; the country, road-trip vibe remains, driven by the sound of the Rhodes piano. However, while the original's string arrangements gave it a friendly, Waterboys-esque feel, this version seems more rooted in the rural landscape of Wim Wenders' "Paris, Texas", which, at the very least, imbues it with genuine emotion."Time", by my dear Tom Waits and taken from the album Rain Dogs, remains completely unchanged; no alteration was needed, as the only shift here lay (significantly) in the vocals. Tom's voice carries powerful tones and deep emotion, tinged with melancholy in this instance, while Tori's version holds its own distinct nuances, rooted in a similarly somber quality but stemming from different sources.Neil Young and his album Harvest need no introduction; they make even those of us who aren't huge fans of country music love it!, And Tori interpreted it as if she were Garbage, with a Portishead-style trip-hop vibe, distorting, transforming, and rocking it out, much like Neil Young had transformed Bob Dylan's "All Along the Watchtower." A double tribute."I Don't Like Mondays", the iconic ballad by The Boomtown Rats (Bob Geldof's band), was a chamber-pop track featuring distinctly New Wave strings, a rich, elaborate sound, and prominent piano work. Tori captured the song's essence while performing solo on the Rhodes; she made it more direct and sincere, less explosive, and instead, something akin to an implosion."Happiness Is A Warm Gun" (originally by The Beatles, of course) features a prominent contribution from Belew, recalling his years alongside Robert Fripp, and evokes the atmosphere of his solo album Exposure, in which the guitar intermingles with audio snippets of George W. Bush; much like Fripp's record, which also incorporated overlaid audio, this concept album cemented modernity as the norm. There is plenty of room for improvisation here, and the creative flight turns progressive once again, with a psychedelic, spacey and cosmic feel.Slayer's "Raining Blood" made people headbang and stomp along to the beat... Tori's version seems to have descended into a netherworld where neither time nor physical matter exists; consequently, it feels and is perceived differently. Her piano is deep and low, it inflicts pain (were we capable of feeling it), and her voice possesses a density equal to that of the guitars in the original. If Slayer's intention was to evoke fear, this version inspires terror.We come to the final track, one by another pianist I greatly admire, Joe Jackson: "Real Men," a classic from his album Night & Day that he always performed live. The original 1982 version already featured a drum machine, keyboards, and an uptempo beat, yet it was imbued with deep emotion through Joe's performance. Consequently, Tori didn't need to alter the song's spirit; aside from performing it as a solo piano piece, an approach she took throughout the album, modifying arrangements only when necessary, she made choices that I feel were spot-on. Just as Joe is a brilliant pianist, so is she; she infused the song with her own piano sensibility, incorporating a few additional classical-style notes. And so, in a manner that feels almost sarcastic given the final track's title and the album's overarching theme, yet while remaining deeply faithful to the defiant spirit of many of the original songs, these twelve covers found a new home.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio format suits the Canterbury scene perfectly. Soft Machine immediately comes to mind, yet a jazz sensibility permeates the French group's sound, whether through the piano or the Hammond organ. As with Soft Machine, vocals are not their strong suit; during the instrumental sections of "Voici la nuit tomb�e," they also lean into a Doors-esque psychedelia.While the classic distorted keyboard sound sets the mood, Yves Hasselmann's vocals occasionally flirt with a classical style reminiscent of Supersister, until the jazz trio element takes over. Atonal passages build great suspense and a French film noir atmosphere, fittingly enough, eventually giving way to further psychedelic sections.However, in other passages, the composition is less daring, settling into a more conventional jazz style akin to that of the previous decade. "Flamenco" follows jazz-style counterpoint, adding Canterbury-esque humor in the vein of Supersister and pushing the sonic boundaries of the trio, with outstanding work from bassist Jacques-Edmond Gour�."Passo" reminded me of Friedrich Gulda's preludes, before shifting into an improvisation more in the style of Keith Jarrett. "Soleil" bears a strong resemblance to Dave Brubeck and "Blue Rondo � la Turk"; the format of short, consecutive tracks suits the trio well following the eighteen-minute suite, as immediacy and speed were Paramount, the idea being that he who strikes first strikes twice, even if they couldn't quite sustain the dramatic tension achieved by their counterparts in Moving Gelatine Plates. The surrealist element was tempered by a classic jazz sensibility that took a bit of the intensity out of the Project, though certainly not its value or quality.
items._genre: Canterbury scene / jazz rock / avant-garde jazz
items._cn_summary: 法国三人组TRAVELLING的1973年专辑以Canterbury Scene为框架，融合爵士三重奏的即兴语汇与迷幻元素。十八分钟同名长曲《Voici la nuit tombée》以失真键盘铺陈氛围，无调性段落营造法国黑色电影般的悬疑感，人声偶尔闪现古典风格点缀其间。短曲集则展现更多爵士向探索：《Flamenco》以对位手法拓展三重奏边界，贝斯手Jacques-Edmond Gouré表现突出；《Passo》在格尔德式前奏与贾瑞特式即兴间转换；《Soleil》明显致敬布鲁贝克《Blue Rondo à la Turk》，节奏紧凑。整体在实验与可听性之间寻求平衡，超现实主义笔法被经典爵士底色适度收束，削弱了部分戏剧张力，但制作品质与艺术价值仍属上乘。
