items.body: When Side-Line spoke with Rina Pavar in 2023, live performance was still something she approached from outside: the studio was familiar territory, while putting herself physically at the centre of the music remained a challenge. Three years later, watching her open Saturday at Nocturnal Culture Night on the Parkbühne, in daylight and before the festival had fully gathered momentum, the change was striking. The restraint was still there, but it no longer read as self-protection. It had become part of the language. That distinction matters because Pavar’s music is built around control in several senses. She writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; her arrangements tend towards clarity rather than accumulation; and even live, the electronic architecture necessarily fixes certain parameters in advance. Yet the more interesting development is how she has begun using that control to create freedom rather than insulation. She speaks here about abandoning perfection as a useful measure, learning that a stage persona does not need to be a separate personality, and discovering that authenticity can emerge gradually rather than through some dramatic act of self-reinvention. That makes the timing of this conversation particularly interesting. Her second album, “six”, appeared in March 2025, followed later that year by “REMIXES”, which handed her tightly controlled compositions to artists including Radondo, Kay-Chi, Skelesys, New Haunts and others. In August 2026, “too much” opened another phase: more direct, more emotionally immediate and, in Pavar’s own words, less subtle. Rather than presenting this as a clean break with what came before, she seems more interested in testing how far the existing language can stretch. The final answer she gives here may be the simplest description of that process: think less, be bolder. Rina Pavar interview Karo: I saw you at NCN only a few days ago, on the Parkbühne, and I was thinking about how peculiar the setting actually was for your music: an early festival slot, daylight, people still arriving and adjusting to the day. Does a situation like that require you to construct your own atmosphere almost against the surroundings, or do you prefer not to impose a predetermined mood on a performance at all? Rina: Yes, that was really unusual. But I always take as much time as possible beforehand to rehearse and visualise the specific setting and the audience. I was familiar with NCN and the Parkbühne from a guest’s perspective, so I could easily imagine what my performance would feel and look like at that time. I think this approach allows me to adapt more flexibly to the circumstances, including in my song selection and the style of my performance. Even though, of course, the core always remains the same, the details change with every performance. Karo: When you spoke to Side-Line in 2023, performing was still relatively new territory for you and the studio was very much the place where you felt most secure. Three years later, I watched someone who seemed considerably more settled within the physical act of performing. What changed? Was it simply accumulated experience, or did you have to discover a different version of yourself onstage? Rina: I think it’s a little bit of both. So far, I still don’t approach the unknown entirely without fear or hesitation. That’s why practice and experience remain the cornerstones of my self-confidence and my progress. My stage persona has also changed over time. But through my experiences so far, I’ve realised that there’s actually no need for a “different” version of myself on stage. Rather, as my experience and self-confidence grow, more space opens up for me to enjoy the performance and let my authentic self shine through. That’s why I take the time to discover and refine myself in this environment bit by bit and at my own pace, instead of artificially building something that I’ll eventually have to shed one day because it no longer fits. Karo: “too much” arrived only a few weeks before NCN and has now been presented as the beginning of a new sequence of releases. Why was this particular song the right point of departure? What does it introduce that you felt had not already been said on six? Rina: I think it has a completely different vibe. It’s more direct, more emotional and less subtle in terms of content, without going completely over the top. At least, that’s how I feel about it. That’s why I thought it was the perfect choice for the first single. I’d actually included it in the NCN set, and the reactions were consistently positive. That confirmed my choice. Karo: six contained a great deal of looking backwards: memory, relationships, places, decisions, versions of oneself that have already existed. I wonder whether your writing is changing now from processing experience towards something more immediate. Are you becoming interested in writing from inside an experience while it is still unresolved, rather than only once you understand what it meant? Rina: For me, it always happens in a flexible and spontaneous way. When certain topics or approaches are important to me at the moment, they naturally take centre stage at that time. But things might look completely different again in the next project. Karo: Because you write, perform, produce and mix your own material, almost every important decision remains with you until the mastering stage. That gives you enormous artistic coherence, but presumably also removes the useful resistance another person can provide. How do you recognise the moment when complete creative independence stops being liberating and starts becoming a blind spot? Rina: That’s an important point. And I’ve often had to listen to all the things that can go wrong when you work on your own. That’s why I’ve found the following approach, which works for me. First, I took the pressure off myself to be perfect, and for RINA PAVAR I decided to focus on presenting what comes from me as a person, regardless of whether it’s perfect, good enough, innovative, trendy, cutting-edge or whatever. If it brings me great joy and meets my standards for growth at that moment, then that’s good enough. This creates freedom and keeps me from getting stuck in a safe, rigid framework. Furthermore, with every release, I set new but achievable goals for myself, whether musically, vocally, personally, in live performances or even just in terms of design. I sit down and teach myself something new or try to optimise processes and recognise patterns to eliminate blind spots as much as possible. Karo: There is considerable restraint in your arrangements; individual sounds are often given enough room to become structurally important rather than being surrounded by layers simply because they are available. Is reduction something you consciously work towards? In other words, do you spend as much time deciding what a song can survive without as deciding what it still needs? Rina: I think that’s one of the few things I don’t have to consciously work towards. When I’m producing a song, I actually have to force myself to add elements. I’m always surprised when someone tells me how clean or minimal the mix is. In my mind, I’ve actually “packed it full”, and I often think to myself, “Okay, there’s room for improvement here, and I should be a little bolder in approaching this aspect.” But reduction, or perhaps “clarity” is a better word, is something that runs through everything I do. For me, it’s fulfilling to break down complex situations to their essentials, to distil the core, to organise, structure or simplify things. And that happens completely automatically. Karo: REMIXES placed your songs in the hands of artists with very different instincts, which is almost the opposite of the control you normally have over your work. Was there a remix that revealed something about one of your compositions that you had not recognised yourself, perhaps because another artist emphasised a rhythm, mood or tension that you had considered secondary? Rina: I’d almost say that’s the case with all the songs. Often, my favourite elements are highlighted but placed in a completely different context or emphasised even more. I love every one of these songs and am thrilled to experience my creations in a more developed and reinterpreted form. Karo: Your collaboration with Kay-Chi on “Darkest Night” is interesting for a similar reason, because there you contributed lyrics and vocals to somebody else’s musical framework rather than building the entire environment yourself. Does writing from inside another producer’s world free you in some way, precisely because you are not responsible for every element of the finished piece? Rina: It’s definitely a challenging yet enjoyable situation. I really enjoy not having to take full responsibility for everything. At the same time, though, I often put pressure on myself to do the parts that I work on perfectly. After all, I want to do the song justice and not disappoint the artist who chose me as a collaboration partner. Even though it may seem overwhelming at first, and it’s not always easy to find my place on someone else’s song, I always look forward to projects like this. It’s fun, offers the chance to collaborate and is always a nice change of pace from working solo. Karo: You also work visually, and I am interested less in whether your visual art “matches” the music than in whether the two forms make you think differently. Music unfolds through time, while an image confronts you more or less simultaneously. Does moving between those two ways of organising an idea change the way you compose? Rina: The way I compose doesn’t change because of this. The approaches and the way ideas come to me are simply too different. But painting is my balance to music, and vice versa. For me, it’s a kind of respite from the other and therefore the break I need to develop and bring new ideas to life. Music is often stirring, full of energy and, despite studio work, takes place largely outside. Painting is absolute stillness, tranquillity, grounding and complete isolation from the outside world. Karo: Coldwave and dark electronic music have developed a very recognisable vocabulary, and recognition can become both an advantage and a trap: listeners know immediately where they are, but artists can also end up repeating gestures simply because those gestures belong to the language of the scene. Which elements of that vocabulary still feel central to Rina Pavar, and which ones have you begun questioning? Rina: If I had to name one thing that remains an important, central aspect, or an indispensable element, for me it would be the melancholy in the sound and lyrics. These are still elements of my songs because I’m still drawn to them. But to be honest, I don’t think about genre at all when I’m composing. I create songs based on the premise that “I have to like it” in order to maintain the greatest possible creative freedom. Karo: Electronic performances inevitably contain structures that cannot be altered as freely as they might be in a conventional rock band, yet the person onstage is responding to something entirely unpredictable: an audience. At NCN, how much were you actually reading the people in front of you? Can their response change the way you deliver a song even when its underlying architecture remains fixed? Rina: I can always feel the energy of the audience, and I try to respond to it as best I can. Even though the set is basically fixed, since it’s tied to a tight schedule, especially at a festival like NCN, I still always leave room within that framework to add or omit details, swap out songs, vary my vocal delivery, let loose and adjust the announcements to be longer or shorter depending on how the audience reacts. At NCN, it was great to see that everyone was fully into it even at such an early hour, and that really gave me power. Karo: Your development so far has involved becoming more confident not only as a songwriter but also as someone willing to place herself physically at the centre of the project. At this point, what would artistic growth actually mean to you? Is it greater musical complexity, greater simplicity, taking more emotional risks, collaborating more, reaching larger audiences, or something that has nothing to do with scale at all? Rina: I want to continue acquiring new technical skills and incorporating them into my compositions. When performing live, I’d like to experiment a bit more, both in terms of the performance and the look, as well as the instrumentation. It’s basically a matter of fine-tuning every aspect to bring out and strengthen the essence of RINA PAVAR even more. Karo: Finally, looking ahead: “too much” has been announced as the first of a series of new releases, so we clearly are not looking at an isolated single. Without asking you to reveal anything that should remain a surprise, what is beginning now for Rina Pavar? And when we eventually look back at this next body of work, what do you hope we will hear in it that was not there before? Rina: I do have an idea of what the “new” element will be in the upcoming releases. But since I’m always worried that listeners might not even notice it, I’d like to start by summarising it this way: Think less, be bolder. About Rina Pavar Rina Pavar is a Leipzig-based German solo project started in 2019. Her own Bandcamp describes the music as coldwave and dark electronic music, while Cold Transmission characterises the project through driving basslines, vintage synthesizers, accented vocals and lyrics concerned with consciousness and personal experience. Her debut album, “vivid night”, was released digitally on 1 November 2021, followed by the EP “things we hide” in May 2022. Pavar writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; those credits are documented on both “vivid night” and her second album. The second album, “six”, was released through Cold Transmission on 21 March 2025. It contains nine tracks and was mastered by Frithjof Rödel at Atomino Studio, with artwork and cover by Pavar and photography by yules_pictures. On 5 December 2025, she released “REMIXES”, a ten-track collection featuring reinterpretations by Radondo, Kay-Chi, Zee Mon, Skelesys, Close Proximity, PJ, Sun’s Spectrum, New Haunts and Three Days Awake by Bent, alongside Pavar’s own club mix of “structured fall”. Pavar also contributed lyrics and vocals to Kay-Chi’s “Darkest Night”, released as part of the Night Protocol EP on 27 March 2026. Her latest single, “too much”, was released on 14 August 2026. Cold Transmission announced it as the first in a series of new releases, marking the beginning of the next phase of the project.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评围绕Rina Pavar的现场表演与音乐理念展开，记录了她从录音室创作者逐步成长为现场表演者的过程。文章以2023年的采访为参照，对照她在Nocturnal Culture Night舞台上的表现，指出她的克制已从自我保护转变为艺术语言的一部分。Pavar独立完成作词、演奏、制作与混音，编曲追求清晰而非堆叠，电子架构虽预先设定参数，却以控制创造自由而非隔绝。她的第二张专辑"six"于2025年3月发行，随后"REMIXES"将作品交由Radondo、Kay-Chi、Skelesys等艺人重塑；2026年的"too much"则更直接、情感更即时。乐评重点呈现她对完美主义的摒弃、对舞台人格的重新理解，以及"少想、更大胆"这一贯穿始终的创作哲学。

items._cn_summary: 本期电台节目精选涵盖广泛的声音探索：Ak'chamel的嘉宾混音带来仪式感与暗色调的实验声响，融合中东/北非神秘主义元素；Bill Orcutt的吉他在《Music In Continuous Motion》中呈现即兴的锐利边缘；Carl Stone的《Auburn》改编版由Arthur Fischl演绎，展现当代作曲与古典诠释的对话。节目还收录了Dur-Dur Band的索马里迪斯科、Upsetters的牙买加dub、Joni Mitchell的爵士民谣，以及Harju、yeongrak等地下厂牌艺术家的作品。整体编排横跨实验电子、世界音乐、即兴与当代古典，体现了电台节目对多元声音景观的开放态度，是发现非主流音乐资源的良好入口。

items.body: Immersion What Is Lost Will Return Immersion find new shapes within familiar sounds, turning repetition into something restless What Is Lost Will Return by Immersion Given the history behind Immersion, it would be easy to hear What Is Lost Will Return as a record looking backwards. That is a useful quality for a band with Colin Newman and Malka Spigel’s respective histories: there is no shortage of past to draw upon. But What Is Lost Will Return feels pleasingly unconcerned with doing so. It occupies a strange, immediate space somewhere between song, groove and electronic abstraction, where guitars, bass, electronics and voices seem to be continually finding new combinations. ‘Nephology’ is a particularly good place to enter this world. items._cn_summary: Immersion 是由 Colin Newman 与 Malka Spigel 组成的乐队，二人此前在 Wire 与 Minimal Compact 等后朋克名团中的经历为这张专辑提供了深厚的底蕴。然而《What Is Lost Will Return》并未沉溺于对过去的回顾，而是将熟悉的元素重新组合，进入一个介于歌曲律动、节奏推进与电子抽象之间的奇特空间。吉他、贝斯、电子声响与人声持续地碰撞出新的搭配关系，使循环往复的素材始终保持躁动不安的状态。文中特别提到开场曲 'Nephology' 以厚重的贝斯脉冲作为入口，展现了乐队在结构与音色层面的巧思。整体而言，这张专辑在保留后朋克骨架的同时，融入了电子与实验性的处理方式，对追求跨界融合与声音探索的听众具有相当的吸引力。

items.body: Uboa releases the live album “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” through The Flenser on 22 September 2026, with a vinyl edition to follow as part of the label’s Membership Series 8 Exclusive. The three-track release is a recording of “Meltdown,” a piece Roadburn commissioned Uboa to compose for its 2024 edition. Uboa’s ‘Meltdown’ performance from Roadburn 2024 Roadburn commissioned Uboa to write two original works for its 2024 festival: “Calm Down,” a quieter piece, and its counterpart “Meltdown,” performed alongside TOomD’s “Shut Down.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend” is the live recording of “Meltdown,” captured from the mixing desk at Roadburn and later remixed and reworked, since some onboard vocal effects and microphones were missing from the available stems. The title refers to Reactor Four at Chernobyl, the reactor that melted down in the 1986 disaster. Musically, the release leans on power electronics and cut-up harsh noise, closer to the extremity of Uboa’s 2018 album “The Sky May Be” than the more intricate construction of her recent records. Uboa described the themes behind the performance directly: “It’s about embracing the overwhelm rather than shaming oneself for it. All the shame, anger and overwhelm was put in this short performance.” She added: “Sometimes it’s fine to just crash the fuck out. Sometimes it is necessary.” The album runs three tracks: “Dys,” “Do Not Comply In Advance” and “Ascension Threshold.” Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024) by Uboa The Flenser also published a full-album stream of the performance: All Bandcamp proceeds from “Every Reactor Four a Friend” go toward covering Xandra’s gender-affirming surgery costs through 21 October 2026. About Uboa Uboa is a solo power electronics and noise project active since 2010, based in Melbourne, Australia. Early releases “Sometimes Light” (2010) and “Jouissance” (2013) were self-released before the 2018 album “The Sky May Be” arrived on the Australian label Art As Catharsis. “The Origin of My Depression” followed in 2019, initially self-released before The Flenser reissued it on vinyl after Uboa signed to the San Francisco label in February 2023. The Flenser then released the 2024 studio album “The Great Impossible Light,” featuring contributions from Blood of a Pomegranate, Otay:Onii, Charlie Looker and Haela Hunt-Hendrix of Liturgy. Uboa performed three sets at Roadburn Festival in Tilburg, Netherlands, in April 2024, including the live debut of “The Origin of My Depression” performed in full alongside the commissioned pieces “Calm Down” and “Meltdown.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” is the recording of that “Meltdown” performance, released through The Flenser two years on.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由Uboa在2024年Roadburn音乐节现场演出的实况录音专辑，曲目源自受音乐节委约创作的作品。录音捕捉自混音台，之后重新混音并修复缺失的人声效果与话筒音轨。专辑标题影射切尔诺贝利四号反应堆，主题聚焦于拥抱情绪崩溃而非羞耻，将羞耻、愤怒与失控感浓缩进短暂的现场表演中。音乐风格回归Uboa早期作品中更具极端性的力量电子与拼贴式刺耳噪音路线，相较近期精致制作更为粗粝。演出中还与TOomD合作呈现了另一首委约作品。收入将用于资助创作者的性别确认手术费用。

items.body: Infrarosso Se mi guardi, cambio forma Come fuoco nell’oscurità Infrarosso Barcelona-based duo VILLANELLE have figured out something plenty of club records forget while staring lovingly at their own machinery: rhythm gets interesting when there is a body inside it. Infrarosso, the debut single from Jessica Bellomo and Carmilla Sioux, runs on that friction. Synthesizers press forward with clean, metallic authority, the bassline prowls beneath them, and the beat keeps tightening the room until Bellomo’s voice becomes another pressure point in the arrangement. Their shared connection to rock and darker electronic music comes through two distinct histories. Bellomo is an Italo-Argentine interdisciplinary artist whose production, DJ sets, and live work span dark disco, electro, breakbeats, EBM, techno, and trance. Sioux began as a bassist in the post-punk scene before moving into electronic music as a DJ and producer, founding From Hell To Disco in 2024. VILLANELLE gives those experiences a shared form, bringing their understanding of club music into close contact with songwriting, visual presentation, and the possibilities of performing together. The writing of Infrarosso began with the instruments. Sioux developed the foundations of the bassline, and Bellomo built layers of synthesizers around it. The music took shape before the words, giving the duo a structure against which to test melodies, vocal rhythms, and different languages. That sequence helps explain the close relationship between the arrangement and the singing: the voice developed through a conversation with sounds already in motion. Traces of Pet Shop Boys appear in the chilly economy, Ladytron in the clipped sensuality, and Boy Harsher in how desire folds into sensual repetition. VILLANELLE draws from their influences without turning the song into a résumé. The bassline has enough shape to carry the track by itself, but the synth layers keep introducing new angles, giving the arrangement a strange sense of forward motion even when repetition becomes the hook. Analog warmth and digital precision meet in a track that keeps its emotional temperature unsettled. Italian gradually became the natural language for the song. Friends independently imagined the instrumental with Italian vocals, reinforcing a direction the duo were already discovering through experimentation. Its musicality, warmth, and sensual undertone suited the track’s character. As Bellomo worked through melodies, spoken-word phrases, rhythm, and rhyme, the provisional title Infrared became Infrarosso. The choice took shape in the act of singing, with the sound of the words helping determine what the song would become. Infrared suggests a presence beyond ordinary sight, something registered through heat when appearances offer little guidance. The opening line, “Se mi guardi, cambio forma”—“If you look at me, I change shape”—adds another complication: being seen can change us. Read as a statement about intimacy, it suggests the strange adjustments people make under another person’s attention, when attraction and exposure become difficult to separate. The title offers a way to sense what remains beneath those changing surfaces. The phrase Sotto la pelle, “under the skin,” became central to the duo’s conception of the track. Bellomo circles a few elemental ideas—heat, skin, darkness, disappearance—and treats language as percussion, stretching words across the beat until meaning and sensation start leaning into each other. The lyrics ask what survives between two people when the world loses light and only sensation remains. There is romance in that image, though VILLANELLE leaves enough tension in the track to imbue that romance with a bit of salt rather than sugar-sweetness. This approach also reflects the poetic dimension behind the project’s name. For Bellomo and Sioux, words participate in the rhythm and atmosphere of a composition, with repetition giving a phrase room to change emphasis. On Infrarosso, the voice works almost as another instrument, adding movement while preserving space for an emotional response. The lyric’s economy allows small shifts in delivery to carry considerable weight; the same words can feel inviting or uncertain depending on how they sit against the beat. Nicole Krämer’s video extends the same fascination with body and machine through darkness, movement, and controlled physicality. It belongs to the broader visual language VILLANELLE are developing around the music, where nocturnal elegance and bodily presence reinforce the tension within the songs. The imagery suits a track built around pressure and restraint, where sensuality comes from withholding as much as release. Read alongside the opening lyric, the camera introduces a further layer to that exchange. A song about changing under another person’s gaze becomes a performance offered to the viewer’s attention. Movement gives the rhythm a visible form, while the words continue to point toward something that cannot be understood through appearance alone. The relationship between music and image grows from that shared concern with what a body reveals and what it keeps private. Watch the official video for Infrarosso below: Live performance has helped the duo understand how these ideas reach an audience. They describe their debut at Stella Nomine as an early lesson in how strongly people could connect with the material while hearing the songs for the first time. Repetition offered listeners a point of entry, while the duo’s physical stage presence and visual interaction added another means of communication. In their account, the response in the room helped clarify what VILLANELLE could become. That experience makes the stage an essential part of the project’s development. A repeated phrase can establish familiarity within an unfamiliar song; a gesture or an exchange between performers can give its tension a visible expression. For music so concerned with perception and proximity, a live setting brings those ideas into a shared space. The audience encounters the people responsible for the sounds, and the performers discover how those sounds affect others. Released September 10, 2026, Infrarosso introduces a duo already thinking beyond one song. An album is planned for spring 2027, with further exploration of the relationship between voice, instruments, electronic production, and the body. Their debut establishes the terms with considerable assurance: post-punk’s rawness, Italo’s melodic appeal, and electronic music’s physical force all have a place in the conversation. The duo describes the intention behind Infrarosso as “music intended to be felt — somewhere beneath the skin.” Across the recording, the video, and their account of performing live, that idea takes a concrete form. A bassline becomes a framework for synthesizers; a voice finds its language inside their patterns; movement carries the song into view. By the time an audience answers, the private sensation has become something people can share. Listen to Infrarosso below and order the single, out now via From Hell To Disco, here. items.body: You said we’d never change You said we’d never fall I held on to every word I believed it all Forever is an ambitious promise to make on behalf of two people who are still changing. Romance encourages this sort of confidence, giving even the most cautious among us the vocabulary of someone who has personally inspected the future. When the relationship ends, those assurances acquire a different meaning, and the person who believed them has to wonder how much of the deception they helped along. Leipzig’s Kalte Steine turns that uncomfortable recognition into the cool, deceptively buoyant synthpop of “Love Is A Lie.” Following the social suffocation explored in “Drowning,” the single brings the question of dishonesty into a more intimate setting, where two people discover that sincerity offers little protection against making promises they cannot keep. A breathy exclamation hangs in reverb as the title refrain begins, with cool synthesizer tones underneath. Bubbly figures and bell-like notes soon brighten the arrangement, joined by a danceable drum-machine beat whose straightforward momentum gives the song its immediate pop appeal. There is an easy catchiness to these parts, each phrase leaving enough room for the next to register. The declaration that love is a lie becomes remarkably easy to sing along with. Buzzing synths and guitar tones gather beneath the first verse, while a brief metallic ripple of programmed percussion adds a small disturbance to the steady beat. The vocal sits high in the register, smooth and quietly sorrowful, carrying disappointment through its tone as much as its words. Deep bass strumming adds weight below, grounding the brighter electronics in the song’s private reckoning. The arrangement keeps moving even as the singer returns to assurances that have become difficult to hear. Initially, the lyrics give that disappointment a familiar address: “You said we’d never change / You said we’d never fall.” Every promise belongs to someone else, and the singer occupies the apparently straightforward position of having trusted the wrong person. The repeated title sounds conclusive enough to close the case. Yet the second verse quietly changes the pronouns: “I said we’d never change / I said we’d never fall.” The same words now come from the person who has been condemning them, making the earlier accusation considerably harder to sustain. “I promised you forever / Like it could be true / Oh I believed it too” supplies the song’s most revealing admission. Both people have mistaken the intensity of a feeling for evidence that it will last. Desire makes the promise persuasive to the person speaking as well as the person listening, complicating the chorus’s sweeping verdict. Through the repeated “Promises,” the post-chorus keeps returning to that shared vocabulary, setting “Words of love / Hearts on fire” beside “A web of lies / Built on desire.” What once sounded reassuring has become a reminder of how willingly both participated. When the chorus returns, melodic guitar figures add detail without crowding the hook, their economical phrasing intricate enough to reward attention and direct enough to stick. A laser-like synth accent introduces a little electronic whimsy, suggesting the beginnings of acceptance within the song’s disappointment. That small, almost playful touch suits a lyric that has gradually surrendered its claim to innocence. By the end, “Love Is A Lie” sounds like something the singer is still trying to believe, perhaps because admitting that the love was real and the promises failed is harder. Listen to Love Is A Lie on Spotify below: Love Is A Lie continues the English-language direction heard on “Crying Out” and “Drowning,” extending a catalogue that also includes “Shattered,” “Dysthymia,” “Wüste aus Beton,” and “Kinder der Nacht.” As explored in our earlier feature on Kalte Steine, the project has moved between personal fracture, urban alienation, and nocturnal escape. Here, its attention settles on the distance between what lovers mean and what they can reasonably promise. items.body: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn. Somewhere behind the electronic throb and serrated guitar on their latest offering, the EATEN OF WORMS LP, there is also the emotional breadth of the Chameleons, a little Breeders crookedness, and that marvelous early-goth conviction on bass guitar. The band began with best friends playing and dancing in a dark Boston basement at the tail end of the pandemic, drawing together members of The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz, and Secret Hearts. They describe this incarnation as their “dark punk chapter,” which sounds about right, though “chapter” seems almost too civilized for music filled with drowning sailors, torn bodies, predatory birds, collapsing circuses, religious dread, and people standing beside freezing seas wondering precisely when existence developed such a personal vendetta. There are obvious ancestral spirits here: Xmal Deutschland, Parálisis Permanente, early Siouxsie and the Banshees, the strange congregation that gathered around the London Batcave when punk discovered it could wear theatrical makeup without surrendering its teeth. They sound less interested in reconstructing 1982 than in asking what happens when those old poisons get poured into present-day arteries. Their live pedigree adds another clue. GOSSIP COLLAR have shared stages with The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime, and Sympathy Flowers, placing them comfortably among bands for whom darkness still needs rhythm, muscle, and enough propulsion to keep bodies moving even while the songs are busy describing spiritual ruin. Throughout the songs on EATEN OF WORMS, nature rarely provides comfort. Seas threaten to swallow people, birds wait for flesh, wolves pursue deer, plants cut skin, rain destroys, and the night contains forces that clearly have not received the memo about personal boundaries. GOSSIP COLLAR’s apocalyptic fairy tale grows out of this collision between childhood imagery and adult terror, where forests, animals, oceans, and old religious symbols have all turned slightly hostile. Edgar Froese once said, “There is no death, there is just a change of our cosmic address.” GOSSIP COLLAR sound perfectly capable of furnishing the house he moved into. Disguise My Heart opens with a saxophone-like drone, its low complaint quickly overtaken by a deep, quick-moving bassline and drums that strike with the urgent physical force of Joy Division’s Love Will Tear Us Apart. The guitars pick out a cold, melodic figure before heavier layers gather around it, giving the song a density that makes the vocal seem to travel from somewhere beyond the instruments. Witchy and windblown, the voice calls through the mix with a banshee’s sense of occasion, stretching the distance between the rhythm section’s forward charge and the solitary figure waiting beside the Northern Sea. Freezing water, aching eyes, and blood threatening to turn cold give emotional injury a bodily presence; the guitars seem to press against the skin as insistently as the memories. Even as the drums push onward, the song remains fixed on that desolate stretch of coastline. Heartbreak becomes architectural here: eventually you stop carrying it around and simply move into it. Scavengers follows with a sheet of cold guitar and an insistent bass throb, burying an unusually inviting melody several layers into the disturbance. When the arrangement briefly catches its breath, the bass leads the voice into view, exposing the sharp, declamatory cadence beneath its witchy inflections. There is an anarcho-punk edge to the delivery, a sense that these words are being hurled across a room even as the guitars make that room feel enormous. That force suits a song whose speaker lies broken, bleeding, and apparently available to whatever happens to be circling overhead. The hook keeps drawing the ear back through the commotion while memories collect like personal debris beside the body. Death may happen quickly, destruction takes its time, and the promise of resurrection supplies a final complication. Apparently even carrion birds are going to have to wait their turn. A brief arc of distortion introduces Big Top Comes Crashing Down, followed by a jagged guitar figure that rings with the blunt insistence of a tolling bell. Once the drums and bass hit, the riff acquires a crooked melodic momentum, turning its initial severity into something almost indecently catchy. Above it, the vocal echoes with a thunderous breadth, making the performance feel much larger than the cramped emotional circumstances it describes. White greasepaint goes on, the smile gets rehearsed again, and another day disappears beneath the effort of remaining presentable. That circling guitar figure becomes an apt accompaniment to the work of doing it all again tomorrow. The image of someone maintaining the same expression for ten years on Exmouth Street carries the ugly comedy of a photograph that has outlived everybody’s patience. Keep smiling hard enough and sooner or later your face becomes part of the prison. Haerisis gives the bass room to announce itself, opening with a thick, deliberate strut locked to the drumbeat. Sustained guitar tones spread above that steady march, and the clearer placement of the vocal lets its chanting insistence register more directly. The arrangement has a substantial physical weight, with dense guitar chords and more melodic lines carrying on around a groove that remains easy to follow through all the theological panic. Blood, broken bones, forbidden chalices, frozen streams, wolves, and deer crowd the lyrics, turning belief into a landscape where almost everything can injure you. The sustained tones lend those images a sense of scale, while the rhythm section keeps their violence close enough to feel. There is something particularly effective about the orderly tread beneath all this religious dread: the song advances with the certainty of a procession whose destination nobody has thought to question. On Dead Thing, a heavy wash of guitar gives way to the splash and momentum of the drums, with the opening density settling into a firm support for the melody. Another weighty riff sweeps through the arrangement, while a persistent guitar drone keeps pressure on the spaces between its movements. The vocal sounds cavernous, its thunderous resonance making each phrase seem to return from the far end of a large, inhospitable room. Those overlapping guitar textures give the song’s fascination with self-destruction considerable force. Lions are led by their manes, weapons are made, and human ingenuity eventually discovers the convenience of turning its own inventions inward. Scars become evidence and shame becomes inheritance, yet the drums maintain enough movement to make the plea for dancing feel entirely plausible. Tenderness enters through the side door wearing funeral clothes, and the rhythm section has already made room for it. Why Me? begins with eerie chimes and a low drone, suggesting an old piano being played somewhere beyond the inhabited rooms of a house. A thick bass figure gradually establishes the song’s tension, recalling the stalking movement of the Cure’s A Forest with considerably more weight behind each step. The vocal holds its heat close, sounding troubled and intimate against the spacious opening. Around the halfway point, heavier guitars enter and the arrangement settles into a cold gothic-rock groove, increasing the pressure while keeping its movements controlled. That restraint gives the lyrics’ grotesque physical imagery additional bite. Red lips, internal screaming, and organs hanging from trees turn desire into a form of captivity, while the bass continues its patient inspection. The fascination directed toward the speaker feels increasingly forensic, as though somebody has been pinned beneath a collector’s glass and asked to appreciate the compliment. The uneasy string-like tones and warbles that open Peaceful in Daylight make its title seem optimistic well before the kick drum lands. Arcs of cold guitar stretch across the entrance, then the full beat pushes the song into motion, carrying heavy riffs and a vocal whose witchy bite grows sharper against the instrumental weight. Seaweed, dense smoke, cutting thorns, broken walls, injured skin, and abandoned nests accumulate in the lyrics, filling the song with evidence that something has gone badly wrong. The arrangement gives that damaged environment a restless physical life; every forward push seems to uncover another unpleasant detail. An old-school rock guitar solo adds a flash of theatrical excess, briefly letting the instrument take over the voice’s fevered work. Daylight may make this place easier to inspect, but there is very little in the music to suggest that inspection will bring reassurance. Spelling Misery initially gives its guitar melody a clear view of the room. The figure rises and falls over a solid rhythm section, its easy memorability providing a point of reference before heavier guitars and dark vocals crowd into the arrangement. Further melodic details appear as the song progresses, with a recurring gothic-rock guitar phrase adding small complications to the surrounding force. Those returns keep the ear attached to the song even as its family portrait becomes increasingly difficult to look at. Anger lives in the blood, a father kills the fatted calf in nervous rage, and memory falters under the effort of naming what has happened. Biblical promises of shelter follow: arrows will fail, feathers will cover the vulnerable body, and fear might be held outside for another night. The returning guitar figure offers a little steadiness amid those appeals, though the heavier passages make the promised protection feel precarious. Unsafe State opens with a buzzing synthesizer pulse and cold electronic tones, briefly suggesting a turn toward synthwave before the melodic resonance of the post-punk guitars establishes its place on the record. The vocal sits more clearly in the mix, and its somber delivery makes the song’s vulnerability unusually exposed. Where other tracks enlarge their distress through dense guitars and cavernous echoes, this one allows the words to feel nearer, with the electronic repetition giving them an uneasy regularity. Eyes lose their rhythm, time becomes a dark tunnel, and the speaker digs until their nails hurt while dead souls call from somewhere nearby. The guitar melody carries that distress with a fragile clarity, giving the song an emotional directness that makes its domestic setting especially troubling. Home is supposed to provide some distance from danger; here, danger has apparently obtained a key. The closing Merchants of the Wave begins with a bassline that shifts up and down, setting a rolling motion beneath a classic post-punk guitar figure. Broader gothic-rock arcs develop around that melody, while the ghostly vocal seems suspended above the rhythm section’s steady movement. The arrangement gives the record’s returning ocean imagery a physical shape: friends venture onto dangerous seas, boats pitch, beds shake with frantic dreams, and tears become indistinguishable from salt water. The bass keeps the song moving beneath those anxious visions, its rises and falls suggesting the uncertain footing of people trying to remain upright. Prayer repeats because repetition may be the only available defense against forces too large to negotiate with. The sea that opened the album as a place of private emotional exposure becomes a shared source of fear here, carrying the possibility that somebody loved might disappear beyond reach. GOSSIP COLLAR keeps returning to bodies under pressure: freezing, bleeding, scratched, exposed, dissected, exhausted, threatened with consumption or drowning. Yet these bodies persist. They dance. They pray. They disguise themselves. They paint their faces. They get abandoned to scavengers and announce plans to rise anyway. Musically, that stubbornness comes through in the combination of deathrock abrasion and electronic precision. Imagine Ladytron discovering a box of Killing Joke singles beneath the floorboards, then recruiting the Chameleons to widen the horizon while somebody from the Breeders quietly rearranges the furniture. Beneath all the gothic architecture runs punk’s ancient belief that anxiety becomes considerably more useful once somebody gives it a bassline. That may be why GOSSIP COLLAR’s particular apocalypse remains so inviting. Civilization has collapsed, the circus tent is falling, the sea wants your body, God may or may not be answering correspondence, and several animals appear to have questionable intentions. Fine. There is still a song playing downstairs. Might as well dance before the scavengers get here. Listen to EATEN OF WORMS below and order the album, out now via Bat-Cave Productions, here. items.body: I recently wrote about an innovation currently taking place in noise rock, where noise rock bands that have embraced everything from more elaborate and thoughtful songwriting to unsettling electronic experimentation on their 2026 releases. Some that I didn’t mention have taken on a spacious, extended approach to the genre while others have embraced a dense, radical brevity. Bands across the genre have been stretching and morphing the style into previously unknown forms over the last few years, but it feels like this year has been especially fruitful in this regard. Tankerlow’s sophomore effort Slagroom can safely be added to the growing list of innovative noise rock that has been released this year, and it stands among the best.On Slagroom, Tankerlow employs a variety of sonic and dynamic approaches. Several tracks slowly unfold with a drone-like quality. There is an openness to those tracks that allows them to breathe and bloom on their own without being forced into a preconceived form by the composers. This natural pacing gives the impression that the members of Tankerlow exhibited considerable restraint, especially within a genre known for its compositional density. This restraint is most prominent toward the end of “Ergo/Ogre” when the song gets so quiet that the listener can hear the buzz of the amp underneath vocalist Guy Azulay’s unsettling, quiet moans. Yet, within that restraint is an impressive, free-wheeling aptitude for experimentation. That experimentation is prominent throughout the album, and not just with the more expansive tracks. Hammered dulcimers, pitched-down looped vocals that sound like a horn, and feedback accidentally created in the studio are all features on the groove-oriented “Formula Baby.” This combination of various compositional approaches and experimentation give each track their own character, a trait that is sadly hard to find in noise rock.What is at least partially responsible for that experimentation is the fact that the band spent over “two consistent and meticulous years in the studio,” which also explains the high quality of Slagroom’s production. Slagroom is, simply put, the best-sounding noise rock I’ve heard all year. Aspects of the album’s mix and sonic qualities oscillate between warmth and intimacy and coldness and harshness. Many of the album's sounds have an industrial quality, but they all come through the mix with analog-like warmth and clarity. Primary vocalist Azulay’s spoken-word vocals on tracks like “DIN” sound as if he is an unwell man standing right next to you on the subway, calmly detailing his mental deterioration in broken sentences. At other times, Azulay’s vocals explode into ranting and raving fury, such as during the tortured refrain in the middle and end of “Plasticine.” The opening guitars on “Ergo/Ogre” are subdued jabs, cutting into the mix like a cold butter knife. But that guitar contrasts wildly with the clanky, claustrophobic walls of chaotic distortion that envelop the listener in the song’s more climactic moments. Other aspects of the production are more subtle, such as the kick drum in “Glory Hole” that suddenly has more gain added to it during the song’s climax. According to the band, Slagroom explores “the concept of duality and the conflicts that arise from the battle of opposites,” and that notion is represented in nearly every aspect of the album. Slagroom is a rewarding but unsettling listening experience in part because the result of so many of those “battles of the opposite” is purgatory — a sense of being perpetually stuck in the gray, struggling to answer questions on identity, capitalism, and fame. But this, along with the experimentation and assiduous attention to detail, is what makes Slagroom such an intriguing listen and one of the most engaging noise rock releases this year. Of all the innovative releases put out under the noise rock banner this year, Slagroom is easily one of the best. SLAGROOM by tankerlow
items._cn_summary: 这是乐队Tankerlow的第二张专辑，乐评将其定位为今年最具创新性的噪音摇滚作品之一。专辑在编曲上展现出极大的克制与自由并存的特质：部分曲目以无人机式的缓慢展开，给予声音呼吸与绽放的空间，末段甚至安静到能听见音箱底噪与人声的细微呢喃。同时，乐队在制作中融入大量实验性元素，包括锤击扬琴、降速循环人声、偶然产生的反馈等，使每首曲目都拥有独立性格。制作历时两年有余，混音在工业感的冷冽与模拟质感的温暖之间游走。主唱Guy Azulay的念白式人声仿佛地铁中旁人的低声独白，偶尔爆发为激烈的嘶吼咆哮，在压抑与爆发之间形成张力。整体而言，这是一张在传统噪音摇滚框架内大胆拓展边界、融合多种声音实验的扎实之作。

items.body: Ryuichi Sakamoto’s score to The Staggering Girl – Luca Guadagnino’s follow-up to Suspiria – is out now on Milan Records. The short film stars Julianne Moore and Sakamoto’s score is a haunting one. Dense textures and off-colour piano melodies bring Aphex Twin’s classic Selected Ambient Works II back from the grave, and gaseous hisses combine with spectral whispers to cut off escape routes, surrounding the music and then gripping it. The interspersed piano notes act as stepping stones. Minimal and yet doing just enough to stay afloat, they bob up upon the music’s surface. A bedrock of static lies underneath. The notes change ever so slightly, preparing for a different scene, wearing a different outfit, delivering different lines, even while keeping the same actress on set, and this creates a melodic continuity. The soundtrack rewards close listening. A blurred synth progression lingers in the background, creating an air of mystery, and undercurrents of light static bring about a shivering unease. Quietly invasive strings stutter back and forth, recalling the work of Hitchcock. A black-and-white mood drapes itself over the strings, growing in suspicion and gradually increasing in tension. The score is a tense one, and there’s a sense of colliding with something shocking and unavoidable, no matter the direction, like Daphne DuMaurier’s Don’t Look Now. The misty atmosphere and the slow, cold synths summon up feelings of dread and paranoia. This is made all the more impressive given the short length of the film. Sakamoto didn’t have the luxury of a longer running-time, and the score has constricted, too, giving it a tighter, more cohesive feel, and being all the better for it. Sakamoto’s skill shows through, because The Staggering Girl feels like a completed work. www.milanrecords.com

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌整理了贝宁歌手Antoine Dougbé与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo在1977至1982年间的合作录音。Dougbé以拍击大腿演绎Cavacha节奏著称，该节奏由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车节奏中提炼，后席卷1970年代中期的刚果流行乐。作为伏都教信奉者，Dougbé仅与Poly-Rythmo合作，认为其他乐队无法精准呈现其构想。专辑收录其三张专辑及若干单曲，展现融合古巴son、刚果伦巴与贝宁伏都传统的独特声音。编曲中合成器与电吉他音色带有八十年代初的塑料质感，但根源律动依旧扎实。部分曲目以合成器铺底，闪亮吉他在高帽驱动的不间断律动上展开对话，后半段吉他分裂向不同方向行进，合成器再度回归形成底层音床。另一首作品则明显倾向古巴风格，固执的牛铃、经典鼻音唱腔与紧凑重复的吉他短语贯穿始终。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的第二张专辑延续了首作的杂糅路线，以自制乐器为核心特色——成员用废旧物品手工打造了多种非常规乐器，包括低音号般的 tubofones、克拉里欧风格的 clarinuts、迪吉里度变体的 didjerimou 以及厨房用具式的 kitchenofon。评论特别指出这些自制乐器在现代录音技术下依然保持了准确的音准和丰富的音质。曲目编排上，乐队按音乐风格匹配乐器配置：克莱兹默曲目以"笑中单簧管"配合巴松管与急促打击乐；昆比亚曲目由长笛主奏搭配西班牙语合唱与拉丁打击乐；阿弗罗贝特曲使用木琴配铃钹，非洲木鱼与沙锤散布于立体声场中。萨姆巴旋律中长笛再度登场，而中东风格曲目则营造出六十年代间谍剧配乐般的恍惚氛围。整张专辑展现了一种从垃圾中创造音乐的理念，评论将其与世界各文化的音乐传统相联系，探讨了音乐创作材料与文化表达之间的关系。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: Camilla Hole Trio 的新专辑《Langs》延续了他们跨文化探索的路线，将挪威西部的传统民间旋律置于爵士即兴的语境之中。Hole 以高音萨克斯为主奏乐器，搭档包括贝斯与鼓，并叠加了模块合成器与颤音琴的色彩层次。三人之间的角色分配并不固定，乐器在旋律与节奏的功能间自由流动。开场曲目取材于西部挪威的 springleik 舞曲传统，旋律先由萨克斯陈述，随后贝斯与鼓展开更开放的即兴对话，萨克斯在尾声再次回归主题。与前作将科幻合成音色与传统素材结合的太空感相比，《Langs》显得更贴近地面，但依然保持着对本土音乐边界之外的好奇。整体展现了北欧爵士乐手在民间传统与现代即兴之间寻找平衡的方式。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

Godflesh themselves have done this twice so far. But it hits differently when it’s a cherished band from your late adolescence.
