items.body: Review by greenpete — They made a startlingly confident beginning with their exuberant, minor-label debut, An Evening With Dando Shaft (no, not a live album). But Dando Shaft's high-water mark arrived with this, their sophomore LP (often called the "Carousel" album, and released on RCA's short-lived Neon label, which only issued 11 albums total). This record dispenses entirely with drums, plunging deeper into varied, lyrical progressive folk. Singer Polly Bolton, from the wonderfully named village of Leamington Spa, joined the boys to bolster their string intricacies with her breathy, Sandy Denny-esque voice. The debut was marred only by the awkward "The Cat Song," but on the Carousel album, there's really not a bad cut. The Bulgarian-rhythmic songs of dual guitarists Dave Cooper and Kevin Dempsey, and mega-instrumentalist Martin Jenkins, are consistently strong, with Jenkins' mandolin, flute, and fiddle shining here. His tune "Whispering Ned," about a gent who enjoys indulging in sugar cubes (and whom the band evidently knew) adds an imaginative twist to the canon of drug songs. The upbeat "Pass it On" is notable for its exuberant chorus about values that have, sadly, since gone out of style. But the real highlights are "Till the Morning Comes" and "River Boat." Both feature Bolton's angelic vocals, the former a wispy duet with Cooper graced by luscious, gently psychedelic flute (Jenkins) and tablas (Ted Kay); and the latter an utterly breathtaking, pastoral delight that conjures green, rural England in poem-song.Bolton would stick around for Lantaloon, a good but inessential album, then depart after tiring of feeling like a "guest" vocalist. So if you plan to only get one album by this highly underappreciated psych-folk band...take a ride on the Carousel.- greenpete
items._cn_summary: 这是英国乐队Dando Shaft的第二张专辑，发布于RCA旗下短命的Neon子厂牌。专辑彻底抛弃了鼓的运用，将渐进民谣推向更精致内省的方向。女主唱Polly Bolton加盟后，以近似Sandy Denny的空灵声线为乐队原有的弦乐编织增添了人声维度。两位吉他手Dave Cooper与Kevin Dempsey的作品融入了保加利亚节奏元素，多乐器演奏者Martin Jenkins的曼陀林、长笛与提琴构成了丰富的器乐层次。曲目整体水准稳定，尤以'Till the Morning Comes'和'River Boat'为代表，前者是一首带塔布拉鼓与迷幻长笛的轻柔对唱，后者以田园诗般的旋律勾勒出英格兰乡村的绿色意象。歌词主题涉及价值观传承与社会观察，编曲在民谣基底上适度实验，整体呈现出六十年代末英国民谣场景向渐进摇滚过渡时期的典型美学。

items.body: Front Line Assembly released their eighth studio album, “Hard Wired,” through Off Beat on 25 September 1995, with Metropolis Records handling North America and Energy Rekords issuing the record in Sweden. It was the Canadian electro-industrial band’s first release for the German label. The album turns 31 this year. Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber produced the record and wrote all ten tracks, which run 62 minutes: “Neologic Spasm,” “Paralyzed,” “Re-Birth,” “Circuitry,” “Mortal” (instrumental), “Modus Operandi,” “Transparent Species,” “Barcode,” “Condemned” and “Infra Red Combat.” Greg Reely engineered and mixed, with Delwyn Brooks assisting, continuing a working partnership that began on “Caustic Grip” in 1990. Devin Townsend played electric guitar, returning after his session work on the previous year’s “Millennium.” Dave McKean produced the illustration, design and photography. The sessions ran roughly five months at the Warehouse. Leeb wrote the lyrics only once the music was finished, and described that order as the band’s normal method rather than a choice made for this record: “We write […] the music and then once we’ve got it finished, then I sit at home and start on the lyrics. I can’t imagine writing any other way. […] I think with our music it’s usually the sounds that inspire us.” On what those lyrics deal with, he set materialism and environmental collapse against the technology driving both: “I think most of the lyrics are basically about man versus technology. Basically, we’re destroying our planet with technology. At the same time, technology is the only thing that can save us. It’s this constant struggle between these two forces that is making us go in whatever direction we’re all going.” That reading runs through the sampling as well. The album draws audio from “True Romance,” “In the Mouth of Madness,” “Lifeforce,” “Stargate,” “Speed,” “The Puppet Masters,” “No Escape,” “Romeo Is Bleeding,” “The Crow,” “Lethal Weapon” and “Alien 3,” alongside sound effects from the 1993 video game “Doom” and passages from three Aphex Twin recordings. “Circuitry” was the album’s only single, released on 31 October 1995. Its limited edition came as a two-CD digipak with remixes by Haujobb and Biosphere, a mixed-mode first disc carrying the “Millennium” video and photo galleries, and a second disc with the non-album tracks “Destructive Transformation” and “Hydrogen.” The album reached number 47 on the Swedish albums chart and the single number 32 on the Swedish singles chart. “Hard Wired” has sold at least 50,000 copies worldwide, and its 5,000-copy limited edition sold out in two weeks. A further track from the same sessions, “Plasticity,” was held back and issued separately; Fulber explained the decision in commercial terms: “We kept it off the album to release later […] It gives people a reason to check it out because if you release it as a single that is already on album no one is really going to care.” The “Plasticity” video won Best Alternative Video at the MuchMusic Video Awards in Toronto in 1996. The album has returned to shelves twice since. Black Rain Records pressed a 500-copy picture vinyl in August 2011, cut to seven songs, dropping “Mortal,” “Modus Operandi” and “Transparent Species.” For the record’s twentieth year, Artoffact Records issued a 300-copy vinyl box in 2015 pairing the album with the “Live Wired” live record and the “Circuitry” single, all remastered by Reely; Side-Line reported that The Front Line Assembly 6LP boxset ‘Hard Wired’ is almost sold out that May, and covered the same year’s news that Front Line Assembly finally see ‘Plasticity’ released on a 10 inch vinyl (3 formats). “Hard Wired” streams on Spotify. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb formed Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, Canada, in 1986, shortly after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had contributed bass synth and backing vocals between 1985 and 1986 under the name Wilhelm Schroeder. He picked the band name to reflect his view that strength lies in working together. The demo tapes “Nerve War” and “Total Terror” were limited to 100 copies each and mostly passed around among friends, with Rhys Fulber contributing as an unofficial member. The project’s first appearance on record was “Aggression,” on the 1987 Third Mind compilation “For Your Ears Only.” Belgian label KK issued the debut album “The Initial Command” at the end of 1987, with Fulber and Michael Balch assisting, and German label Dossier released “State of Mind” in January 1988. When a planned Nettwerk release fell through, Third Mind put out “Corrosion” and the “Disorder” EP later that year, then signed the band to a three-album deal and licensed “Corrosion” to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch became an official member in 1988 and left after the 1989 “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” tour to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks. Fulber replaced him and appeared on “Caustic Grip” (1990), the album that started the band’s long partnership with engineer Greg Reely and introduced guitar on “Provision” and “Resist.” Chris Peterson debuted as live percussionist on the tour that followed in early 1991. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) turned toward more melodic, multi-layered arrangements and the heavy film sampling that became a fixture of the sound. Five remixes for Fear Factory’s “Fear Is the Mindkiller” EP in 1993 fed directly into “Millennium” (1994), the band’s first industrial metal record, built on metal guitar samples and Devin Townsend’s session work. “Hard Wired” arrived the following September. Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on production, and Peterson took his place for “FLAvour of the Weak” (1997), “Implode” (1999) and “Epitaph” (2001), a run that traded the metal influences for breakbeat and big beat. Fulber returned for “Civilization” (2004), and Peterson rejoined for “Artificial Soldier” (2006), the first album to feature Jeremy Inkel and Jared Slingerland. “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021) followed, the last on Metropolis. The band also composed soundtracks for the games “Quake III: Team Arena,” “AirMech” and “WarMech.” Inkel died on 23 January 2018 at the age of 34, from complications of an asthma condition. Leeb has run Delerium since 1987 and Noise Unit since the late 1980s, while Fulber started Conjure One after his 1997 departure and has worked with Fear Factory for decades; Side-Line published a Front Line Assembly interview – Catching up with Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber in 2024. “Hard Wired” turns 31 this year, the record that closed out the guitar-driven stretch the band opened with “Millennium” before the electronics took over again.
items._cn_summary: Front Line Assembly 第八张录音室专辑《Hard Wired》于1995年发行，由Bill Leeb与Rhys Fulber共同创作制作，十首曲目贯穿62分钟。专辑延续乐队典型的电子工业路线，制作流程上以音乐先行、歌词后置为创作习惯。歌词主题聚焦于技术与人类之间的张力：既是摧毁地球的力量，也可能是唯一的救赎。采样方面大量取材于九十年代电影对白与音效，包括《True Romance》《The Crow》《Alien 3》等作品，并融入《Doom》游戏声效与Aphex Twin段落，构筑出浓厚的赛博朋克氛围。Devin Townsend贡献电吉他演奏，Greg Reely继续担任录音混音工程。发行依托德国小厂牌Off Beat与Metropolis Records，瑞典榜单成绩中等，累计销量超过五万张。整体呈现了一部融合电影采样、机械节拍与反思性主题的工业电子作品。

items.body: Like many others, my gateway into the Coltrane universe was the inevitable Blue Train , a 1997 CD reissue, with the cover altered with different tones from the original edition. I was beginning to discover jazz and, beyond the variations on the title track, it was the vertigo of “Moment’s Notice” that must have won me over at that early stage. And, of course, the free sound of the saxophone, and the fascinating process of its discourse construction in real time — fascinating for someone who, until then, knew nothing of any form of improvised music. From there, there were several landmark records, in a process that did not follow chronology: it went through the duet with Johnny Hartman, Live at Village Vanguard , the space journey of Meditations , all the way to the devotional magic of A Love Supreme , reading the booklet while following the music, and the pinnacle of Ascension . Along the way, an unavoidable landmark, Giant Steps (as with Ornette’s records, the title also announced the jazz that was coming) with its timeless title track and the melancholic sweetness of “Naima”. I was discovering the albums in no particular order, finding the records or having them find me in a random way, and then gradually organizing Coltrane’s journey in my head, as if piecing a puzzle together. In that process, my favorite album then remains my favorite to this day: My Favorite Things . Too mainstream, too easy, some might say. On ’Trane’s path, a milestone. Not yet the classic quartet, but almost there: McCoy Tyner on piano, Elvin Jones on drums, Steve Davis on bass (Jimmy Garrison would join shortly afterwards). Coltrane takes up the soprano saxophone and transforms a well-known popular melody into a piece of his own; starting from the original melody, he transforms it through a profound process of unfurling. From this point on, it would become one of his signature tunes, evolving into other, much more advanced and deconstructed versions. But this is the start. The LP setlist also has three songs that touch the soul of anyone who loves the history of jazz: one by Cole Porter, “Ev’ry Time We Say Goodbye”, and two by the Gershwins: “Summertime” and “But Not for Me”. In the context of Coltrane's quest and discography, My Favorite Things is a turning point. And, in my own listener's journey, it's music that affects me deeply. Nuno Catarino is editorial coordinator of jazz.pt since 2022. He contributes to the national newspaper Público, where he has written since 2007. He is the author, with Márcia Lessa, of the book Improvisando (2019). Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评并非针对专辑本身的音乐分析，而是作者回忆自己逐步接触Coltrane音乐世界的个人化旅程。从最初的《Blue Train》入门，到逐步深入《Meditations》《A Love Supreme》《Ascension》等自由爵士与精神爵士里程碑，作者特别钟情于《My Favorite Things》——这张标志着Coltrane从硬波普转向调式探索的转折之作。文章详细描述了Coltrane如何将流行旋律解构重组，高音萨克斯在经典曲目中展开自由的即兴话语。评论带有浓厚的个人怀旧色彩与情感共鸣，强调爵士乐历史中经典唱片对听众的深层影响。

items._cn_summary: 这是一张日本四人乐团的全主流首张专辑，以浓厚的后朋克气息贯穿始终。尖锐锐利的吉他音色与极简留白的律动形成鲜明骨架，歌词中穿插颜文字等松散口语元素，在冷峻与玩味之间制造张力。作品涉及城市生活描写、轻快前行的鼓励以及夜色中的情绪停滞等主题，早口演唱与轰鸣吉他制造冲击段落，可爱叙事又适时放松张力，整体始终保持另类姿态。作为主流厂牌发行的另类摇滚作品，其制作指向明确定位，但创新性受限于流媒体推广路径，尚未展现出更加先锋的探索。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由打击乐手Joe Hertenstein领衔的Future Drone乐队录制于维也纳Porgy & Bess现场。虽然编制包含风琴，但乐队并未拘泥于传统爵士风琴三重奏的套路——最初是包含低音提琴的四重奏配置，Hertenstein将Tony Williams的Lifetime作为重要参照，这意味着作品在节奏驱动与即兴能量上更接近融合爵士与自由即兴的领域。作为Hat Hut厂牌的录音，专辑定位偏向学院派爵士与实验即兴的交叉地带，Live At Porgy & Bess的现场环境也为音乐增添了即兴张力与不可预测性。原文因篇幅过短，无法获取更多关于具体编配、和声走向或特殊技法方面的详细信息，但厂牌气质与乐手背景足以说明这是一张面向小众即兴音乐受众的作品。

Clothing: Omar Afridi X VUJA DÉ There is a particular kind of light that only exists after rain has finished falling but before the sun has arrived – a grey-gold hour where the wet ground holds more colour than the sky. Space Afrika has always made records that live inside that hour. Honest Labour, the pair's breakout 2021 statement, was full of it: shortwave murmur, tower-block wind, the feeling of being simultaneously inside a crowd and entirely alone. Five years on, Joshua Tarelle Reid and Joshua Inyang return with Quiet Storm, a record that... The post Shared Frequency: Quiet Storm by Space Afrika appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 曼彻斯特双人组 Space Afrika 携新专辑《Quiet Storm》回归，大幅扩展了此前作品的音色调色板，引入弦乐、竖琴以及多位特邀嘉宾的合作。他们一直擅长捕捉雨后初霁时分那种潮湿地面反射色彩的光线质感，新作延续了这一氛围基调但更加丰沛。此前在《Honest Labour》中以短波噪音、塔楼风声塑造的孤独与人群交织感，在这张唱片中进一步展开。两位成员 Joshua Tarelle Reid 与 Joshua Inyang 通过大量协作者将原本较为内敛的电子声响推向更立体的器乐编制，在实验电子与环境音之间寻找新的平衡点。乐评以诗意的视觉意象开篇，试图为读者建立这张专辑的情感坐标，但正文内容在此处戛然而止，未能深入展开对具体曲目或制作手法的讨论。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Out of Central/East Serbia's most ancient city Nis, comes this fusion quartet that is lead bypianist Ilijic, a competent rhythm section and an electric guitarist that is looking to run awaywith the spotlight. They can make you think of a GoGo Penguin trio with an added electric guitarist,and the least we can say is that they hold this flattering comparison quite well.A live album, encompassing most of Eyot's studio discography, as the recordings rank from '15 to '23 and tracks played from their hometown Nis all the way to Munich and even New York and O-Yokohama.Some Balkan gigs and Western Europe gigs are also present in this selection. As you've guessed,we're dealing more with some kind of "best of" live, rather than a whole concert set list. Over thetwo disc (just under one hour each), you'll be bombarded with some brilliant instrumental interplay,though there is a sense of repetition over the full listen, but one track features a two-horn, whichis a welcome sonic change, if only temporary. IMHO, listen to only one disc at a time, because anoverdose is around the bend.
items._genre: jazz fusion / jazz rock / progressive fusion
items._cn_summary: EYOT是一支来自塞尔维亚古城尼什的四重奏，以钢琴为核心，融合爵士摇滚与器乐即兴风格，编辑将之与GoGo Penguin相提并论。这张双碟现场专辑收录了2015至2023年间在尼什、慕尼黑、纽约、横浜等多地的演出片段，跨越巴尔干与欧美舞台，构成一种精选式的现场回顾，而非单一完整音乐会。唱片中器乐互动频繁且展现出一定水准，配器中偶尔加入双管乐配置，为整体音色带来短暂变化。不过完整聆听两张碟会带来重复感，乐评建议分次聆听以避免听觉疲劳。整体而言，这是一支具备即兴功底与跨界气质的东欧爵士融合乐队作品，但在实验性与声音设计层面未展现出更为突出的突破。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A longtime Jazz veteran of Brasil's music scene catches the "fusion" bug, travels to the USA to collaborate with some of New York City's finest studio musicians. The album was recorded in 1970 at A&R Studios in New York City and then released by Cobblestone Records sometime later in the year.1. "Coalhada (Yogurt)" (3:00) big band jazz that happens to use electric piano. This sounds like Doc Severinson's late night band with Johnny Carson. The song's end is a fadeout during some very animated and dynamic full-band interplay. Nice full-band cohesion. (8.875/10)2. "Hermeto" (4:22) sounds like a Eumir Deodato and Burt Bacharach team rendering of "You Are the Sunshine of My Life." Hermeto's electric piano play fits so nicely over the Smooth Jazz orchestral arrangement. Nice lead flute solo from (probably) Hermeto himself. (9.125/10)3. "Guizos (Bells)" featuring Googie Coppola (6:20) gentle, atmospheric jazz stripped down to Ron Carter, Hermeto's sensual electric piano, Airto's cymbal and brush play, with Flora Purim's wordless vocalese floating within and above it--and, later, a breathy flute. The orchestra makes its presence known in bigger and bigger ways toward the end of the fourth minute, swelling just before Hermeto's sexy little keyboard dance duet with Ron. Flora and low brass return around the five minute mark, prompting the horn-led orchestra to swell again. Beautiful music (that reminds me very much of the intro "Storm at Sunup" section of Gino and Joe Vannelli's opener to their great 1974 album of the same name)! (9.12510)4. "Flor Do Amor (The Love Flower)" (5:51) opening with a beautiful small chamber arrangement of wind instruments that turns to strings for support and takeover around the 20-second mark before melding together to support a lovely lower register flute lead. The harmonic orchestral support is wonderful! Brass take over in the lead position of the "dance," giving Hermeto time to get situated at his electric piano for a turn. Then it's back to flute for the end of the fourth minute, back to keys for the fifth, dueling/dueting with flute (there are so many accomplished flute players credited in the line-up chart that it's hard for me to believe that Hermeto doesn't use one or more of them to play off of: Hubert Laws! Joe Farrell! Jerome Richardson!) (9/10)5. "Alicate (Pliers)" featuring Flora Purim (4:00) this one sounds very much like a Burt Bacharach song with the orchestra providing most of the melody leads for the first 1:45. Then an odd almost "bass" or bamboo flute enters, playing really low, really breathily. This must be Hermeto due to the Amazonian flavor/flare being presented here. Return to orchestral dominance for the rest of the third and fourth minutes (with lots of wonky, animal-sounding brass), and then fade out. (8.875/10)6. "Vel�rio (Mourning)" featuring Flora Purim (8:38) organ, bass, and low-end flute(s) and female vocalese open this one while a taped recording of tribal conversation plays beneath. The whole vibe here is one of the Amazon jungle. Even the violins that enter in the middle of the second minute and the other orchestral instruments seem to be trying to capture or emulate jungle noises. Then in the second half of the third minute Airto's lone violin-like berimbau goes completely solo, sounding like the fast-rushing of an on-coming railroad train. The fifth minute sees a return of the wooden flute (heavily reverbed), which plays solo for a complete minute before petering out and being supplanted by a faded-in piano--who continues the on-rushing train theme--until the end of the sixth minute when the orchestra's trumpet section announces itself sharply, being joined by other brass, winds, strings, and percussion instruments in a very theatric motif that begins to "fall apart" like a drunken debauch at the end of the eighth minute. The chaos is then displaced by piano, bowed bass, and tambourine playing an "old-fashioned" barroom jazz bit to the song's end. Interesting! Not my favorite but I appreciate the creativity behind the song. (17.5/20)7. "As Marianas (The Marianas)" (4:34) full orchestra playing music that sounds like the warm up music to a grand ball or art museum exhibit. This may be jazz (of the Nelson Riddle-Glen Miller kind) but it's nowhere near anything I'd apply the Jazz-Rock Fusion term to. It's also kind of lame, like a sleepy, sloppy version of "Born Free." (8.375/10)8. "Fabiula" (3:51) more "old" strings-dominated cinematic music that may be big band created (I hear the individual instruments like flutes, horns, and Spanish guitar) but it, again, fails to even come close to the musics I would term "J-R F" (or any other kind of fusion). Maybe "orchestral-bossa nova lite" would best describe this soporific fare. At least this one is far more sophisticated and melodic than the previous disaster. (8.875/10)Total time: 40:46B/four stars; Oh! how one really poor song can drag an entire album down from near-masterpiece status to good/worth your attention. Side One is definitely deserving of all your Jazz-Rock Fusion enthusiasm whereas Side Two may bore you to tears--especially if you have an aversion to languorous strings-dominated orchestral jazz and attempts to replicate the sounds of the jungle using musical instruments.

items.body: Review by WizardGirl420 — I write this review in 2026 of an album I listened to extensively when it was released in 2008. Iremember listening to it nonstop for days on end. for years I couldn't listen to THE BEDLAM INGOLIATH without feeling transported in time to 2008-09. So I put it away, so I could live in thepresent.Recently I decided to pick up this album again. It still feels vital. so full of energy. At thisstage in their career the Mars Volta were firebrands of creative energy, one of the leading lightsof the 00s prog rock revival. Their well-earned Grammy win for WAX SIMULACRA, a lead single fromBedlam, was the crown to commemorate this creative peak, before they eventually declined and splitinto assorted side projects. (the followup, OCTAHEDRON, is a significant drop in quality in myopinion, which I don't think they ever got much better from. But I digress.)The album opens with a slam with "Aberinkula". The Mars Volta's trademark complex, salsa-influenceddrum patterns and highly effected guitar is a relentless blast of rocking. I love Rodriguez-Lopez'sguitar style, there's the noisiness from his experience in hardcore punk, but he's obviously verywell-versed in jazz and latin styles with a healthy dose of psychedelia. The heaviness barely letsup as the album smoothly flows into "Metatron". Everything flows together smoothly, actually; thedynamic and mood shifts between the songs feel so natural."Ilyena" is my personal favorite. Extremely catchy, and the electronic noise gives you a nice breakfrom the punk-influenced intensity that defines the album. The rest of the album follows a similarstyle of punk heaviness, electronic distortion, prog rock composition and latin rhythms. Veryunique, very catchy, very loud and very gripping.FRANCES THE MUTE and DE-LOUSED IN THE COMATORIUM might be overall better, and have probably beenmore influential on subsequent prog-minded artists. But THE BEDLAM IN GOLIATH remains a personalfavorite of mine and I think is a great piece of 2000s heavy.
items._genre: heavy prog / latin-influenced prog / experimental rock / psychedelic

items.body: Review by alainPP — Green Carnation presents the third album in the "A Dark Poem" trilogy, nodding to the likes of Anathema and Katatonia. It delivers an oppressive, heavy, and meditative sound with dark progressive roots."Unconditional Artificial Chemistry" opens with a spacey feel, suddenly cut through by an exuberant, thick, heavy guitar; the monolithic vocals help transport the listener to another planet. The track narrates the dangers of AI, unfolding seamlessly while building an all-encompassing, progressive intensity. It shifts to include a crystalline piano in the distance, with musical grandeur that straddles the line between doom and Opeth-esque gothic metal, creating an oppressive atmosphere. There is a spellbinding melancholy'a blend of Anathema, Mogwai, Katatonia, and early King Crimson. "The Messiah Complex" features a melting guitar arpeggio, with vocals that abruptly break the ethereal, charming, and hypnotic mood. Melancholic, mysterious keyboards add a layer of solemnity that oozes progressive structure, while the dominant vocals allow the mantra-like atmosphere to spill over. The decrescendo finale is simple and effective'steady and unstoppable'serving as a musical paradigm."Broken Souls, Common Enemies" features a prominent New Wave-style synth driving the rhythm. The riff, the languid vocals, and the guitar's plaintive melody evoke emotion, discovery, and complexity in a track that is heavy without flaunting it. A shift to screamed vocals over a machine-gun riff'reminiscent of The Gathering in their early days'reasserts the track's intensity and complexity, bolstered by Wright-esque keyboards. A break featuring an ethereal flute and a melting, Western-style acoustic solo follows. Vocoded vocals amplify the majestic atmosphere, launching a stratospheric guitar solo worthy of the genre's titans'a truly stunning moment. Finally, "A Dark Poem - Orchestral Suite" begins with otherworldly vocals introducing wind instruments'including Ingrid's flute'as the orchestral arrangement takes center stage. An orchestral suite worthy of *Fantasia*'a classic pastoral anthem recounting Rimbaud's "Ophelia," performed by the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra and its opera choir. Then comes the break: a return to archaic vocals, a primal sound reaching its zenith'is this the birth of prog? A dark, unsettling, yet colorful and pastoral atmosphere, pierced by illuminating trumpets; it is a masterpiece right up to the final note, with a soaring violin flourish creating a moment that transcends time.Green Carnation takes its final bow with this triptych finale'punchier, spellbinding, and invigorating. It is a crowning achievement, blending dystopian lyrics about our society with majestic, solemn melodies. Classy, ​​dreamlike, and immense progressive post-metal'featuring a sound that left an indelible mark on me from their very beginnings, delivering a powerful impact this September.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Green Carnation《黑暗诗篇》三部曲的终章，融合了Anathema式的忧郁氛围与Katatonia、Opeth式的哥特金属沉重感，并融入Mogwai的后摇情绪张力。专辑以AI为主题展开叙事，开篇曲目在空灵合成器与厚重吉他riff之间切换，营造出压迫性的冥想氛围；中段引入新潮合成器驱动节奏，配合嘶吼人声与机枪式riff，展现出The Gathering早期的复杂层次；终曲则由Kristiansand交响乐团与歌剧合唱团演绎兰波《奥菲利亚》的管弦乐组曲，融入笛声、小号与铜管段落，从原始人声到恢弘弦乐，构建出跨越时空的牧歌式终章。整体呈现出从赛博反乌托邦到古典恢弘的跨度，是一张融合前卫金属、当代古典与暗潮氛围的跨界作品。

items.body: I’ll always wait for you The promise that someone will wait forever has enjoyed an excellent reputation in love songs, considering how uncomfortable it can become outside them. Patience can deepen into devotion, but it can also give obsession an alibi, allowing someone to call an inability to let go proof of a superior kind of love. London trio Black Doldrums explore that uneasy territory on Waiting, a song whose tenderness comes with the unnerving suggestion that nobody has agreed on when the waiting should come to an end. The third single from Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club, carries a particular connection to the band’s previous album. Written around the same time as In Limerence, it extends that record’s preoccupation with longing and romantic fixation into a love song that sounds both consoling and quietly bereft. Its accompanying video takes those feelings out into the city, where a solitary attachment becomes an increasingly threatening pursuit. A deep, humming bass and the heavy thud of drums establish the song’s measured pace, while a cool, jangling guitar melody moves between high, glassy notes and lower, mournful phrases. There is something of The Chameleons in the guitar’s arcing melodies, and of The Cure in the funereal weight beneath it. Sheets of icy synthesizer widen the space around the instruments, giving the opening a peculiar calm: everything sounds composed, even as the melody suggests that something has gone terribly wrong. When Kevin Gibbard begins singing, the synthesizers settle into warmer mid-range tones, bringing a little bodily comfort to that cold room. His voice carries some of Andrew Eldritch’s solemn authority in a slightly higher register, with an exposed ache that also recalls Ian Curtis. Beneath him, the guitar takes on an increasingly Cure-like character, its clear notes ringing against the low end. Then the chorus rises into “I’ll always wait for you,” stretching the promise into a lament. The guitar’s answering jangle supplies the small, involuntary chill, the sort that travels up an arm before the mind has decided whether the feeling is pleasure or dread. For all that unease, the song began in an ordinary moment of affection. Gibbard wrote the lyrics early one morning while waiting for Sophie Landers to wake up, with the themes of their second album still close at hand. “When we were going through the finished mixes of the second album, Sophie noticed this recurring theme of limerence, which pushed ‘Waiting’ further in that direction. I liked the idea of writing about waiting for someone you love, that if you love someone enough, you’ll wait forever. I wrote all the lyrics in one go, early one morning, while I was literally waiting for Sophie to wake up. I just started jotting it down.” Landers also supplied the idea behind one of the recording’s stranger details, asking for a sound that would suggest a spirit departing its body. Gibbard found his approximation through a Mellotron, voice synthesizers, and pitch bend: “Sophie wanted something that sounded like a soul leaving someone’s body. So I played around with a Mellotron and voice synths with pitch bend to create something similar. It seemed to fit nicely because it has this really haunting sound.” That imagined departure hangs over a song devoted to staying. The warmer synthesizers offer closeness, while the guitars and spectral vocal textures suggest distance, absence, and the possibility that a promise might outlast the person it was made to. There is considerable romance in Waiting, though very little reassurance that romance will make anyone happy. The video’s darker premise took shape during a recent viewing of Taxi Driver. Landers recognized connections between the film and the band’s interest in limerence, particularly its treatment of loneliness, idealization, mental distress, and destructive fixation. Black Doldrums developed those observations into a story about an isolated, obsessive man following a woman through the city, with his sense of control destined for a nasty correction. Gibbard and Landers occupy a nocturnal world of café booths, shuttered shopfronts, graffiti-covered brickwork, and stretches of nearly empty pavement. He sits alone with a cup, writes on a loose sheet of paper, and eats in a café; she walks through the streets in a black leather jacket, occasionally looking back. The editing brings their separate movements into an uncomfortable relationship, while red-lit close-ups of her eyes interrupt the greenish darkness outside. The ordinary business of getting through a night begins to feel charged with the possibility of being watched. As the distance between them closes, the action moves into a narrow pedestrian underpass, its fluorescent lights leaving little room for either figure to disappear. Landers walks ahead while Gibbard follows, until a look back changes the balance between pursuer and pursued. The closing image gives heartbreak an abruptly physical form, making the familiar business of giving someone your heart seem like an offer best considered carefully. Watch the video for Waiting below: Gibbard and Landers formed Black Doldrums in London, initially working as a duo built around guitar, drums, and vocals before expanding into a trio. Their 2022 debut Dead Awake and 2024 follow-up In Limerence, both released through Fuzz Club, brought their early interests in psychedelia, drone, and reverb into a more concentrated gothic post-punk form. Extensive UK and European touring followed, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headline shows. Repetition Compulsion completes the band’s interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” exploring the emotional patterns people carry into relationships, memory, and self-understanding. Across eleven songs, the record expands those concerns into inherited behaviour, politics, and mental wellbeing. Waiting provides a particularly intimate connection between the trilogy’s final two chapters, holding affection and fixation close enough for their resemblance to become unsettling. The album arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. Listen below and order via Bandcamp. items._cn_summary: Black Doldrums的《Waiting》延续了伦敦后朋克的阴郁传统，歌曲围绕等待与执念主题展开。创作灵感来自主唱Kevin Gibbard清晨等待爱人Sophie Landers醒来的真实瞬间，歌词一次性写就，捕捉了爱恋中那种令人不安的执着。配器上以深沉的贝斯和厚重的鼓点构筑节奏骨架，清澈而哀婉的吉他旋律在明亮高音与低沉吟诵间游走，合成器层铺陈出冰冷空旷的音场。人声带有Andrew Eldritch式的庄严权威与Ian Curtis式的裸露痛感，副歌将承诺拉伸为挽歌。整首作品在抚慰与丧失感之间摇摆，将个人情感投射为一种渐趋威胁性的城市追逐意象。

items.body: The Red Garland Quintet Featuring John Coltrane and Donald Byrd - Soul Junction (Prestige, 1960) Culinary writers frequently refer to comfort food. Soul Junction is my comfort music. I go to this album when I’m not in the mood to be blown away by wild flights of improvised fury or complex compositions or arrangements. This is an “end of an exhausting day” or a “reminder that maybe all will be well” kind of an album. I love the relaxed, bluesy feel of it. Listen to Garland’s piano on the opening title track. It’s pure bliss. George Joyner’s bass is understated perfection. The piano trio portion of the track goes on so long and is so hypnotic that you’re to be forgiven if you forget there’s a sax and trumpet still to come. Hey, there’s the saxophone. It feels like Trane was digging Garland’s playing and was dying to join in. Recorded in 1957, Trane hadn’t perfected his style yet. But his genius is right there to hear. He’s fantastic on Dizzy’s classic Birk’s Works . Donald Byrd doesn’t get much mention on this website, but I love a lot of his Blue Note music. He’s the perfect trumpeter for this session. Garland wisely gives the two of them lots of space to play, and they take every advantage of it. John Coltrane- First Meditations (For Quartet) ( Impulse!, 1977) As far as I’m concerned, A Love Supreme is the greatest jazz album of all time and Coltrane’s classic quartet the greatest group. First Meditations (For Quartet) is a beautiful piece of music and a fascinating document of a band just on the verge of transforming, both in terms of its personnel and its approach to music. (I prefer to say “transforming” to “ending”.) The first track, Love, clearly recalls A Love Supreme, as if that classic album is the starting point of this new music. Trane is stunning as always and McCoy is the perfect accompanist. The best track, Joy, is relatively calm and peaceful, until it isn’t. It begins as any number of other tracks from this quartet and then Trane sits out. He’s let the remaining trio play some (for this group) fairly straightforward piano trio music. But then he returns with an absolute roar, as if he wants to break constraints the rest of us can’t see. This is one of several places you can see the seams of the band starting to tear. It’s fascinating to hear. Much of this music was reconsidered on the subsequent album Meditations with Trane’s new group. A comparison of the two albums and the approach of two different groups to the material is fascinating, the second album justifiably being the more renowned of the two. But I find the first to be the one I keep returning to, as if I don’t want to say goodbye to this quartet. I genuinely love this album, but I had an ulterior motive for writing about it here. It gives me the opportunity to tell the story of the time I met Elvin Jones. He had been doing a drum demonstration and a line formed afterwards for autograph seekers. When I arrived at the front of the line, I barely refrained from doing “We’re not worthy”, but I did tell him how much his music meant to me and said I’d be honored if he’d sign this album. He took the CD booklet from me, looked at it and asked “Did I play on this?”. (I assume that since the album wasn’t released until 10 years after it was recorded, he never saw the album cover.) I showed him his name in the booklet, he laughed and signed it, making this album all the more special to me. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于两张约翰·科尔特兰专辑的乐评合集。第一张《Soul Junction》是雷德·加兰五重奏1957年的录音，以蓝调抒情基调呈现放松舒适的氛围，钢琴与低音提琴构建催眠式律动，科尔特兰早期尚未成熟的萨克斯与唐纳德·伯德的小号在加兰的克制编排下获得充分展现空间。第二张《First Meditations》记录了科尔特兰经典四重奏向自由爵士过渡的关键时刻，开篇呼应《A Love Supreme》，平静段落中突然爆发的萨克斯咆哮预示着乐队的瓦解与转型，与后续加鼓手拉希德·阿里版的《Meditations》形成有趣的对照。文字穿插了作者偶遇鼓手埃尔文·琼斯的个人回忆，为乐评增添了人文温度。两张专辑横跨硬波普到精神爵士的演进，虽非纯自由爵士，但展现了科尔特兰音乐语汇从传统向实验过渡的脉络。

items.body: (For Now We See) Through A Glass Dimly Deeply rooted in the soul of North Wales, (For Now We See) Through A Glass Dimly echoes and reverberates in and around the nestled villages, working its way through the tiny, crooked streams and the gently stirring brooks of shallow water. Past the twisted knots of the branches, so like a tangling of auburn hair, the music gently progresses into the woods. Musically vibrant, muscularly strong and fit, the music has a fiery power in its stirring string sections, which dynamically rise and then forge ahead like a thousand soldiers consumed in battle, as fierce as the flames of a dragon as its forks streak across the setting sun, matching up with the orb’s blood-orange colour, emerging from a time out of mind. The vocals of Joanna Swan (Ilya) are softer, slowly riffling through the cottage’s windows on a low spring breeze. A tiny brook hides the piano’s melody, but then the strings suddenly burst into life, shining like the sun as it slowly (but inevitably) rises over the hills, unhurriedly beginning a new day. The piano gives way to the swelling strings, and they eventually tower over everything, fortifying the sound with their brass-plated armour, increasing its density. The landscape of North Wales doesn’t just seep through the music – it is the music. It always has been… Imbued in the music is the country’s spirit, her legends and her musings. Like a rock stuck in the side of a mountain, her spirit is wedged there. The grass that spreads itself over the body of the land darkens to a deeper green after a spattering of rain (that’s an intrinsic part of life in the UK, too), and the music of Antonymes (Ian M. Hazeldine) has a similar, vibrant purity in its colouring. The crests of the melodies rise like ancient hills, this long walk in the countryside taking the listener past a beauty that fills the eyes and the ears. There are no shortcuts. It has a rhythm of breathing, on the one hand living in the present moment, and on the other hand telling stories of centuries past. (For Now We See) Through A Glass Dimly is a nascent flower emerging into its perfect bloom, its intense timbres as rich in colour as the surrounding woodland, tonally overflowing like a running river after the rain has fallen; constantly renewing season after season, never ageing. The strings evoke the British weather and its intense, largely unpredictable periods, the brooding, bruised and leaden clouds giving way to cold spells of rain. Its minimal heart conjures a pure, enchanting kind of classical ambient music, a sound as natural as the landscape that shapes and shelters it, the melodies flowing over the grass, the leaves and the forget-me-nots. The music should just be there; its place in the world doesn’t need to be questioned. For a brief time, the piano is left on its own. The strings, descendants of royal blood, fall away, leaving only the piano to fill the space with its plaintive notes. At times sorrowful, the notes start to swirl lazily, supported by a late breeze that’s fatigued by the time evening comes. The strings wear a golden halo, a metallic crown engraved with secret symbols. The seasons shift with the sweeping, slightly grimy fog of the coda, ‘Through A Glass Dimly’. The breeze has a cold bite, and the burning leaves begin to smoulder. They go through their beautiful decline, transforming into bursts of orange and red that reflect the sun’s setting and its inevitable renewal. Autumnal in its feel it may be, but the countryside never really changes. And the music remains crisp, sparkling with an emerald’s clarity, imbued with a shade of deep green that rivals the countryside. Available through Stashed Goods www.antonymes.co.uk
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以北威尔士的自然景观为创作根基，弦乐与钢琴交织出浓郁的地域气质。弦乐编排强劲有力，层层推进如千军万马，又兼具铜管般的厚重质感；钢琴则在关键时刻退居一旁，以简洁的音符填补空间，形成沉思的呼吸感。人声来自Joanna Swan，轻柔如春风掠过窗棂，与宏大的弦乐群形成鲜明对比。整体结构遵循自然的节奏——呼吸、潮汐、季节更替——而非传统的曲式逻辑。音乐继承了威尔士的传说与精神内核，将乡村的忧郁与壮美转化为声音文本。弦乐暗喻英伦天气的不可预测性，从阴郁到骤雨，情绪层次分明。这是一张将地理与人文深度融合的当代器乐作品，适合在沉思与聆听之间展开。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

Adios K
items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?
items.label: Go' Danish Folk Music
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自丹麦三人组合 GuldGanger 的首张数字 EP，由北欧民谣场景中经验丰富的歌手 Mia Guldhammer 主领。五首曲目大多基于传统音乐素材，乐手各自带入不同的个人诠释，整体笼罩着一种古老、质朴的氛围。开场曲《Svennedal》以粗犷的奔跑节奏展示 Guldhammer 极具说服力的嗓音；口簧与风笛在《Nordgård》中提供强烈的推进感，该曲也是乐队成员 Morten Musicus 唯一的原创作品。传统曲目《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》以扬琴铺设细腻背景，收尾曲《Orms》则作为器乐曲融合口簧、长笛与弦乐，营造出颇为奇特而令人兴奋的失衡感。这张作品展现出一个已经相当成熟的乐队起点，其传统根基与乐器搭配暗示着未来更完整专辑的潜力。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由挪威Taragot厂牌发行的跨界专辑，由一位瑞典小提琴家和两位挪威乐手组成。乐曲素材主要源自挪威和瑞典的民间舞曲，但演奏方式并非传统风格的简单复现，而更接近室内乐的对话感——三位乐手在音乐中进行亲密的即兴交流。评论指出这种演绎不适合舞蹈伴奏，而是对民间旋律深层含义和暗流的探索。小提琴家Mats Edén专长瑞典民间音乐并融合多种风格，录音管演奏者Tellef Kvifte曾在七十年代跨界乐队Slinkombas担任先驱角色，其子Knut Kvifte Nesheim作为鼓手也在模糊流派边界。三人的合作展现了斯堪的纳维亚舞曲表面欢乐之下暗藏的不安与复杂，专辑以Setesdal河谷的一首与水妖有关的小提琴曲开篇，暗示这种文化中音乐的魔力与危险双重性。整体呈现出对北欧民间传统的实验性重新诠释。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / documentary sound art
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自芝加哥南区的田野录音作品，由录音师Ian Brennan在街头实地录制，记录了二十五位枪支暴力幸存者的声音与故事。参与者年龄从十七岁到六十七岁不等，包括即兴说唱片段与社区环境声，呈现的是未经任何后期音乐加工的真实声响文档。录音地点位于中途机场降落航道下、靠近密歇根大道繁华区的被遗忘社区，背景中的蚊子声、街头犬吠与受访者哽咽的叙述形成强烈反差。一位失去两个儿子的长者在采访中反复道歉，而评论指出真正该道歉的是造成这种统计性不公的社会结构本身。所有收益将捐赠给以公共卫生方法遏制暴力的Cure Violence Global组织。作品具有田野录音与声音艺术的实验特质，但并非传统意义上的音乐作品，其价值更多在于社会纪录与声音人类学层面。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A reunion, of sorts, in effect as all participants in this studio product had played with Jack in former bands; The Graham Bond Quartet (Bruce & McLaughlin), The Graham Bond Organization (Bruce & Heckstall-Smith), and Jack's previous album, Songs for a Tailor (with Hiseman). (Hiseman and Heckstall-Smith had, of course, been playing for a couple years together in David Greenslade's Colosseum--three albums worth.)1. "Over The Cliff" (2:56) a quick riff from Dick Heckstall-Smith's tenor sax launches bassist Jack Bruce and drummer Jon Hiseman into a rapid-paced expression of fairly straightforward Hard Bop Jazz. There is little to no input from John McLaughlin's guitar but Dick, Jack, and Jon are more than up for the trio presentation. Interesting and respected but this is not really my preferred type of music. (8.875/10)2. "Statues" (7:35) more blues-based Hard Bop Jazz from Dick, Jack, and Jon in which the trio dance around one another in tight and attentive circles, each playing their own consistent melody lines--Dick even going for the two-saxes in the mouth at the same time trick a couple times. In the fifth minute there is a cease and desist order so that Jack can bow his bass a bit, but then Jon rejoins with meagre little input from Dick (and, interestingly, none from John McLaughlin) before Jack steps back to let Jon have the spotlight a couple of times before the recapitulation of the opening themes over the final 35 seconds. Fine musicianship. (13.5/15)3. "Sam Enchanted Dick" - medley (7:28) bass and electric guitar recite the song's main melodies over Jon's drums for the first 30+ seconds before John is loosed with his distorted tone to solo for about a minute. Then it's Jack's turn in the third minute. John's chord accents are all I can pay attention to (for I am a HUGE fan of John's fascinating "rhythm guitar" choices). At 3:37 we hear the first squirts of Dick's, tenor sax--which leads, of course, to an extended solo for him (and yet my ears still find themselves paying attention to John's caustic chord interjections). Double saxes for a bit in the seventh minute before Dick's play on "Sweet Georgia Brown" lead to the song's finish. (13.5/15) a. "Sam Sack" b. "Rill's Thrills"4. "Born To Be Blue" (4:26) a gorgeous ballad with very sensitive performances from all four players. There is enough space in the soundscape of this song that I can very much appreciate the skills and creativity of each individual musician--which I need from time to time in order to better understand and value the musics I'm being exposed to. (9/10)5. "HCKHH Blues" (8:59) there is an auspicious threat of power and havoc in this song's music from its very opening. Despite Jack and John's pulling tendency to want to drift over into the Louisiana Bayous, Dick and Jon do a great job in keeping the spirit firmly anchored in less Southern traditions, more in the urban forms of expression. Finally pusuaded, John and Jack swing over to join Dick and John in their Coltrane-like explorations. (18.125/20)6. "Ballad For Arthur" (7:42) pensive bass notes are embellished by delicate cymbal and snare play while Dick explores his own melody ideas. There is enough focus in Dick's playing that Jack and Jon both feel empowered to let their own playing go a bit into the realms of improvisational freedom--until, that is, John feels inspired to join in (around 1:50). Thereafter John's "commanding presence" effects a stoppage from Jon (no drums or cymbal sound for over a minute!) while Dick tries to figure out how to play background accompanist role to John's spacial musings. With Jon's boisterous Jack DeJohnette-like return in the fifth minute, we find the other three suddenly inspired to become quite a bit more dynamic: each flying off in their own directions while somehow it all still manages to make sense from a collective view. With a minute left to go there is a sudden buildup and burst into controlled chaos before everybody backs out, spent. While I still don't "like" this kind of music, I understand anad appreciate the discipline and skill required to make it happen--to make it work. (13.5/15)7. "Things We Like" (3:38) another this time more targeted and speedy foray into the reactive/responsive side of Jazz' free jazz movement. There is a playfulness to this one that makes it a bit more amusing and, thus, enjoyable. (8.875/10)Total Time 48:04Despite the presence (and influence) of metamorphosizing guitarist John McLaughlin on four of the album's seven songs, the rest of the band on this album (Bruce, Hiseman, and Heckstall-Smith) are all playing Jazz, standard, blues-based Jazz albeit at times what we've come to call their own versions of "free jazz." John is the only one pushing boundaries, injecting non-standard sounds, riffs, and epithets. One might also argue that Dick Heckstall-Smith is pushing for more free jazz representation. Were I more of fan of straight Jazz (I'm trying, folks!) I might like this album more. As it stands, I feel hard-pressed to even consider this "Jazz-Rock Fusion" much less call it such.B+/4.5 stars; while Jazz afficionadoes might consider this a minor masterpiece of Jazz (or even Jazz-Rock Fusion), would call this a near-masterpiece and not a true representative of Jazz-Rock Fusion; to my mind Things We Like has got far more of the fire and focus of pure Jazz than it does of Fusion or progressive rock.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑集结了多位在六十年代末英国爵士摇滚圈有过交集的乐手，以硬波普爵士为基础框架进行即兴演奏。贝斯手Jack Bruce、鼓手Jon Hiseman、萨克斯手Dick Heckstall-Smith与吉他手John McLaughlin组成四重奏，曲目多为中短篇幅的即兴展开，结构相对松散但保留了波普传统的对位与轮奏逻辑。McLaughlin的吉他偶尔参与，更多时候作为节奏声部提供和声点缀；Heckstall-Smith的次中音萨克斯承担旋律主导，常以双嘴含簧片技巧制造特殊音效。慢曲Ballad段落留出充足空间让四位乐手各自展示，节奏曲目则在急促的riff推进中穿插贝斯拉弓段落与鼓手独奏。整体呈现的是七十年代初英国爵士圈对硬波普传统的延续与微调，并未真正踏入前卫或实验地带。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Early (First Wave) Jazz-Rock from Poland. This band's debut, we find them experimenting with blending several styles including Blues-Rock, Psychedelia, Procol Harum-like prog, orchestra-enriched lounge music, and more. The album was released in 1971 by Polskie Nagrania Muza.1. "Sen (A Dream)" (3:17) what feels like an ANTHONY PHILLIPS guitar piece opens this for the first 1:07 before a pause unleashes a bouncing organ chord, funky bass line, and Michael Giles-like drumming with simplistic guitar riffs over the top to announce the presence of melody. In the final 30 seconds there is this all out burst of WHO-like energy being expressed/expelled by all of the band members--which then seems to bleed/lead into the SANTANA-like frenzy that is the next song. A three-part suite in three minutes! Wow! (9.333/10)2. "Kuszenie (Temptation)" (3:29) the SANTANA-like percussion-driven full-band jam that features everybody flying at full speed. Maciej Gluszkiewicz' organ impresses as do the performances of all of the quartet members. (9.25/10)3. "Nerwy Miasta (The Nerves Of Cities)" (3:31) a slowed down PROCOL HARUM-like sound palette that comes off sounding like something from a Blues-Rock band like anything lead by vocalist ALEX LIGERTWOOD, Billy Gibbons, or 21st Century Polish band LIZARD. At the very end the band do a quick shift into high gear for minute of rousing organ-led instrumental fun to finish things off. (8.875/10)4. "Senne Wędr'wki (Wandering Dreams)" (3:52) orchestra-supported blues rock! Interesting! Quite like the sound of PROCOL HARUM. Nice imagination! (9/10)5. "Taniec Wariatki (The Madwoman's Dance)" (2:02) rock-infused theatric cabaret music (almost musique concr'te) with interesting call-and-response playfulness between the instrumentalists. Quite creative. (4.625/5)6. "Taniec Czterech (The Four Men's Dance)" (1:37) fun/funny open air, city green music by the local marching band. Nice drumming. (4.375/5)7. "Na Przek'r (Against Everything)" (2:16) opens like some folk rock from one of the Summer of Love's outdoor music festivals--with vocals (DON BREWER-like lead with Gospel church choir backing), like a. moralistic hippy musical. (4.625/5)8. "Nasze Myśli (Thoughts)" (5:10) pensive four chord progression arpeggiated by guitar with organ, drums, and bass backing while lead singer croons like a South American folk singer singing through the city center's public address system (or else LIZARD's Damian Bydliński). The very pleasant and comforting song contains a somewhat-spirited organ solo but is really just more of a nice ballad. Interesting vocal weave at the finish. Reminds me of 1990s QUIDAM. (9/10)9. "Mrowisko (The Hive)" (4:15) unusual opening with drums and organ playing cat-and-mouse-in-the-mirror for the first 35 seconds. Then a pause opens the door for a classical guitar and intermittent bombastic "symphonic" bursts of accompaniment and antiphonal response--something that gets drawn out for a minute, stumbling and fumbling, until finally fully developed at the three-minute mark. From there we get a minute of song with singing. Weird. (So like the 21st Century music of Polish band LIZARD). Yet interesting. And creative. (9/10)10. "Pejzaż Z Pustych Ram (Landscape Of Empty Frames)" (4:31) gentle electric guitar musings accompanied by responsive ghost-vocalese open this before a fully-meted song presents itself at 1:10. Singer Marek Alaszewski sounds like Jacques Brel during the delicate verse, but then things amp up for the chorus, Marek switching voice tones to something more RPI like as choir vocals chase him around like a church choir. Nice bass work from Roman Pawelski as the band and vocalists sustain the chorus intensity from here to the song's end. Very nice: emotional. (9/10)11. "Taniec Głodnego (The Starvelling's Dance)" (2:24) PROCOL HARUM palette and slow militaristic pace as organ swirls, drum and bass keep funereal time, and wooden flute (recorder) presents and carries the lead over the top. The opening motif switches into something more dance-oriented at 1:38 as Roman shifts to a walking bass line. Sounds like a wonderful night for a Moondance (Van Morrison)! Nice! (4.5/5)12. "Epidemia Euforii (Epidemic Euphory)" (3:46) not sure what is meant by this song's title, but the music feels more derivative of a combination of early British Rock and the U.S.'s Beatnik styles. By the time the band really kicks into full gear we're presented something that sounds more like Steve Winwood's first band, The Spencer Davis Group, as well as, at the percussion end, like The Chicago Transit Authority (with, of course, the Damian Bydliński lead vocal voice). (8.875/10)13. "Sen (A Dream)" (1:49) all four members of the rock combo are here represented with Marek dusting off his recorder again to muse over the gentle/calming nature-backed music. (4.375/5)Total time 41:59A very creative band of proficient musicians who create an unusual but very pleasing style of progressive rock: their songs are either isolated vignettes of imagination or conglomerations of such all smashed together. The bottom line is: that it works! I especially like the interesting use of choral backing vocals and full-spectrum and active percussion tracks.A-/4.5 stars; a collection of what feels like experimental and highly-idiosyncratic musical ideas coming from a very creative and skilled quartet of young musicians that results in a minor masterpiece of early progressive rock music. (There is little or no Jazz much less Jazz-Rock Fusion here).

items._cn_summary: 这是一张1971年波兰乐队的首张专辑，融合了蓝调摇滚、迷幻摇滚、普罗克尔哈穆式的前卫风格以及管弦乐丰富的休闲音乐元素。乐评逐曲分析，指出开场曲在三分钟内呈现三个不同风格段落，吉他与风琴的对话、Giles式鼓击、Santana式打击乐驱动形成对比。慢速作品展现类似Procol Harum的和声色彩，弦乐支撑的蓝调摇滚颇为别致。部分短曲呈现戏剧化卡巴莱风格与城市绿地的行进乐队趣味，体现出乐队在多种风格间自由穿梭的能力。后半段有南美民谣风格的沉思慢歌，以及古典吉他与交响化爆发交织的标题曲，显示出一定的实验意图，但整体仍以摇滚框架为主，未真正深入前卫或爵士融合的边界。

items.body: Review by Thomas1969 — Every time Steven Wilson releases a new album, I think: "Wow, is it that time again?" It also occurs to me that I rarely revisit the albums released after *Hand. Cannot. Erase.* (2015). While every album since then has certainly contained good songs, none have gripped me the way the dark *Grace for Drowning* (2011), *The Raven That Refused to Sing (And Other Stories)* (2013), and the aforementioned album did.What I've missed since then is a certain emotional depth in the music, as well as that "moody" side. Fortunately, we hear that moody side return in the advance track "Requiem for a Village," taken from the album of the same name due out in November. The album cover certainly looks promising. But what about the content?the music itself? "Requiem for a Village" is vintage Wilson: a moody opening, an enigmatic progression, a guitar eruption three-quarters of the way through, busy drumming, and?this is where the real tension lies for me?the quieter passages and mysterious vocals (Wilson is singing more beautifully than ever) at the beginning and end, accompanied by evocative keyboard sounds.Of course, there is a full band behind Steven Wilson?it could easily be called the Steven Wilson Band. Who makes up the band as of 2026? Lead vocals, bass guitar, guitar, Mellotron, keyboards, percussion, piano, oboe, mixing engineer, lyre, producer: Steven WilsonGuitar, backing vocals, synthesizer, Mellotron, co-producer, lyre: Randy McStineDrums: Russell HolzmanSo, it is very much a Steven Wilson affair, but Randy McStine and?most certainly?the new drummer Russell Holzman deserve special mention. They play skillfully?you have to hand it to them?but does it truly *connect*? Does it move me? Richard Barbieri moved me with every keystroke; of that, I remain absolutely certain. I am also left with a nagging feeling?since a new The Pineapple Thief album is coming out next month as well?of whether I am looking forward more to *that* album (featuring Gavin Harrison on drums) or to the new Steven Wilson release. You might say: you still miss Porcupine Tree. That's true. You never really get over that. But what I miss most is the emotional depth found in Porcupine Tree's music. Since *Hand. Cannot. Erase.*, no full Steven Wilson album has truly moved me in the same way. That could change. It might... You probably grasp my point. My ambivalence.A bit of a mixed bag, then, this sprawling track?clocking in at 7 minutes and 56 seconds.

items._cn_summary: 评论聚焦Steven Wilson新专辑同名先行单曲，这首近8分钟的曲目延续了他标志性的阴沉氛围开篇、神秘人声编排，中段出现吉他爆发与密集鼓点，前后段则在键盘铺陈中维持内省张力。乐队阵容以Wilson本人为核心，吉他手Randy McStine与新鼓手Russell Holzman为辅助，但评论者对后者能否真正触动情感持保留态度，更怀念Richard Barbieri时代的键盘质感。整体评价暧昧而克制，指出作品在情绪深度上有所回归，但与Porcupine Tree时期相比仍有距离，并坦言对同期Pineapple Thief新专辑（由Gavin Harrison参与）抱有更多期待。

items.body: Review by Finnforest — "After the Darkness, the Light" On their third and final album of the 1970s, Salis flipped the script once again, sounding nothinglike their previous effort five years prior. The Salis brothers were back, but they had a newdrummer and keyboardist in the lineup, and they obviously were hell-bent on forging a new direction.There is no sign of the debut's personality or the acoustic mellow vibe of the second. Here the bandhas shifted to that largely instrumental spacey fusion sound so common in the late '70s. The first reference that jumped into my mind was PFM's "Jet Lag" album, and I wondered if that wasan influence for Salis here, though "Jet Lag" is more adventurous than this. The mix of polishedrhythm section and quirky keyboard parts also reminded me just a bit of some of the instrumentalinterludes on later Cat Stevens albums. Another band this reminds me of is Finch. If you were intothem, you should enjoy these competent but sometimes tedious instrumentals. There are some very coollead guitar passages in several tracks. I suspect the approach is the reason why this album is ratedso much higher than their previous two, but frankly I don't see it. Yes, the longer jams overfloating keyboard atmosphere is going to appeal to progressive rock fans, but I think thecompositions on the first two albums are more interesting to me. Nevertheless, it is withoutquestion another good album by Salis. It all comes down to your tastes, naturally. I find this albumcompetent but pretty forgettable.
items._genre: rock progressivo italiano / instrumental fusion / space rock
items._cn_summary: 这是意大利前卫摇滚乐队SALIS在1979年发行的第三张也是最后一张七十年代专辑。与前两张相比，乐队阵容发生了变化，加入了新鼓手和键盘手，音乐方向也大幅转向以器乐为主、带有漂浮键盘氛围的太空融合风格。评论者将本专辑与PFM的《Jet Lag》、Finch以及Cat Stevens后期器乐段落相比较。专辑中包含若干出色的吉他独奏段落，长篇幅的器乐jam段落配合键盘氛围铺陈。该评论者认为此专辑在ProgArchives上评分高于前两张，但个人更欣赏前作中更有意思的作曲。整体而言，这是一张技术能力扎实、偏向器乐氛围融合的作品。

items._cn_summary: Lustmord Lombardo 的专辑《The Pulse of Atoms》在 Ipecac Recordings 厂牌下发行，乐评试图将其定位为超越时空界限的声音作品。评论指出这张专辑难以归类于任何特定类型或时代——它既不属于去年，也不属于十年前或二十年前，更不属于未来，仿佛在尝试悬置于时间之外。这种描述暗示了作品具有强烈的氛围感和冥想性，通过极端缓慢的律动与厚重的低频构建沉浸式的黑暗空间。Ipecac 作为以实验和前卫发行著称的厂牌，进一步印证了作品在声音探索层面的取向。整体而言，这是一张面向深度聆听者的氛围工业作品，注重质感与空间感而非旋律结构。

items.body: Soft Riot has finished a video for “Ghostwriter,” the closing track on the 2026 album “Crux.” It is the project’s second official video from the record, following “Moving Out Of The Black,” which premiered at the end of April 2026 ahead of the album’s release on 15 May. A premiere date for “Ghostwriter” itself is still being finalised; the video is not yet public. Crux by Soft Riot Jack Duckworth, who records as Soft Riot and is also known as JJD, built the video’s visuals as a graphic, surrealist collage rather than a straight performance piece, with puppet-like character animation reflecting the song’s theme: the sense of ideas for “Crux” materialising, as though something unseen were “ghostwriting” the record. All of the animation was made by hand from physically printed graphics and re-filmed projected textures, a deliberate move away from computer-based tools that Duckworth has linked to feeling increasingly isolated within the digital side of underground music. Duckworth handled all graphics and editing as JJD, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. “Ghostwriter” closes a nine-track album written and recorded across several sessions between June 2024 and January 2026 at Studio Carillon in Glasgow, with vinyl mixing by Owen Pratt at Flesh And Bone Studios in Tarn, France, and mastering by Josh Stevenson at Otic Mastering. “Crux” is available on streaming platforms, as a download through Bandcamp and Subvert via Possession Records, and on vinyl and digipak CD, including a limited clear vinyl LP on Minimal Kombinat that sold out within a week of pre-orders. A follow-up EP, “Alter,” released in June 2026, carries exclusive, alternate and extended versions of “Crux” material. About Soft Riot Soft Riot is the synth project of Jack Duckworth, a British-Canadian musician based in Glasgow who has released music under the name for around fifteen years, drawing on synth post-punk, darkwave, new wave, Italo and EBM. Duckworth’s roots go back to the mid-1990s art-punk and hardcore scene on the North American west coast, where he played in the first-wave post-punk revival band Radio Berlin (1998-2005) and the industrial synth-punk group A Luna Red (Gold Standard Labs, 1999-2003). As Soft Riot, he has toured Europe repeatedly, sharing stages with acts including Front 242, Absolute Body Control, Parade Ground, She Past Away, Test Department, Selofan, Drab Majesty and Lebanon Hanover, and has played festivals including Ombra Festival in Spain, BIM Fest and Waveteef in Belgium, Kalabalik På Tyrolen in Sweden and Weird Science in Germany. Side-Line has previously covered the Soft Riot albums “You Never Know What Might Come Next” (2016), “The Outsider In The Mirrors” (2018) and “When Push Comes To Shove” (2019), followed by “No.” (2023) and, in 2026, “Crux” and its “Alter” companion EP.

items.body: Delerium released the single “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, on 23 September 2026 through Metropolis Records. It is the first single from Delerium’s new album “Exaudire”, set for release on 22 January 2027. Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) by Delerium “Into The Light” incorporates portions of “Deliver Me From Mine Enemies”, written and performed by Diamanda Galás and included on her 1986 album “The Divine Punishment”, the American avant-garde singer’s Mute Records release that opened her “Masque of the Red Death” trilogy. The Delerium track sets that material inside the group’s own production, credited to founding members Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber. “Exaudire” follows Delerium’s 2023 album “Signs” and carries twelve tracks, continuing the group’s format of pairing largely downtempo, atmospheric songwriting with a rotating cast of guest vocalists: Higher Power (with Mimi Page) Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) Dream Palace (with Magic Wands) Buried Light (with Mimi Page) Apocalypse (with Inna Walters) Stolen (with Phildel) Into The Unknown (with Jaël) Multiplying Zero (with Inna Walters) Chasing The Wind (with Mimi Page) Exaudire Had To Go (with Jaël) Litany (with Mimi Page) About Delerium Delerium was founded in Vancouver, Canada, in 1987 by Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber, both already active as members of the electro-industrial group Front Line Assembly. Where Front Line Assembly carried the pair’s aggressive, rhythm-driven material, Delerium became the outlet for their dark ambient and instrumental compositions, released through Dossier and Third Mind before the project moved to Nettwerk for its commercial breakthrough. From the mid-1990s onward, starting around “Semantic Spaces” (1994), Delerium began inviting guest vocalists to front largely downtempo songs on each album, a format the group has kept since. That approach produced its best-known track, “Silence”, featuring Sarah McLachlan, which reached number three in the UK singles chart following a series of 2000 remixes and won two Juno Awards for Best Dance Recording. Delerium music has since appeared in films including “Brokedown Palace” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider”, and “Silence” featured more recently in the BBC drama “Industry”. With Front Line Assembly already on the Metropolis Records roster, Delerium signed to the label for the albums “Mythologie” (2016) and “Signs” (2023). “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, is the first taste of the follow-up, “Exaudire”, due on Metropolis Records on 22 January 2027.
items._cn_summary: Delerium 即将发行新专辑《Exaudire》，首支单曲《Into The Light》与美国先锋歌手 Diamanda Galás 合作，将后者 1986 年专辑《The Divine Punishment》中《Deliver Me From Mine Enemies》的片段重新置入 Bill Leeb 与 Rhys Fulber 的制作框架内。整张专辑延续了 Delerium 长期以来的模式：以降速、氛围化的电子骨架为基础，搭配多位客串歌手轮流主唱，包括 Mimi Page、Magic Wands、Inna Walters、Phildel、Jaël 等人，共收录十二首曲目。从信息来看，制作延续了乐队标志性的暗潮电子路线，与 Diamanda Galás 的合作是本次最值得关注的前卫元素，但专辑整体仍属既定公式的延伸，未见明确的突破方向。
